title: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
summary: Capture traffic at scale, read pcaps, filter in Wireshark, pivot through Zeek logs, tune Suricata rules, fingerprint TLS with JA3 and JA4, find beacons and DNS C2, extract files and work a real infection.
outcomes: Choose between packets, flows, Zeek logs and alerts for a question, and size capture storage and sensor placement
Read a pcap file's headers and write Wireshark display filters that avoid the any/all and existence traps
Pivot through Zeek's conn, dns, http, ssl, x509 and files logs with uid, fuid and Community ID
Explain how Suricata content modifiers, sticky buffers and EVE flow_id work, and tune noisy rules
Compute JA3 and JA4 from a ClientHello and explain what JARM, JA3S and default certificates reveal about C2
Score beaconing with robust statistics and find DNS C2 and tunnels per domain, as in the SUNBURST case
Extract and type files from traffic safely, and run a network investigation from first alert to scope

lessons.title: Packets, flows and logs: three kinds of network evidence

blocks.md:
**Network traffic analysis** is answering questions about what happened on a network from records of its traffic: which machine talked to which, when, how much, and what they said. **NSM** (network security monitoring) is the practice of collecting those records all the time, so the answers already exist when an alert or an incident arrives.

Tiny example, taken from the Zeek documentation: a workstation at 192.168.4.37 downloads a 179 KB Windows program over plain HTTP. The same download can be kept in three very different forms:

1. **Packets**: all 222 packets (93 from the client, 129 from the server), every byte: about 198 KB as a pcap file.
2. **A flow record**: one line saying 192.168.4.37 talked to 23.195.64.241 on TCP port 80, how many packets and bytes went each way, and when.
3. **Transaction logs**: three short lines from Zeek saying the client asked `download.microsoft.com` for `wfetch.exe` with a `Wget` user agent, got status 200, and the body was a Windows executable.

blocks.title: One sensor, four kinds of output

scenes.caption: A passive sensor receives a copy of the traffic (lesson 2 covers how). Everything an analyst later knows about the network comes from what this box chose to keep.
Full packet capture keeps every byte in pcap files. It answers any question about content, but it fills disks fastest, so it is kept for days.
Flow records (NetFlow or IPFIX, from the prerequisite course) keep only who, when and how much. Tiny, so they can be kept for months, but they never show content.
Zeek writes transaction logs: one line per connection, DNS query, HTTP request, TLS handshake or file. Far smaller than packets, far richer than flows.
Suricata writes alerts when traffic matches a rule. Alerts point at the moment to look; the other three stores say what happened around it.

blocks.md:
Each form answers different questions:

- **Packets** answer everything the wire carried: the exact bytes of a request, a file that was downloaded, a password sent in clear text. They cannot read inside encryption any more than you can.
- **Flows** answer *who, when, how much, how often*: enough to spot scanning, beaconing and large uploads, cheap enough to keep for a year.
- **Transaction logs** answer protocol questions: which DNS names were looked up, which URLs fetched, which TLS server name and certificate were offered, which files crossed the wire and their hashes.
- **Alerts** answer *did anything match what we already know is bad*. They are only as good as the rules, and they say nothing about traffic no rule describes.

This course teaches the three tools that produce most of this evidence in open-source shops: **Wireshark** for packets, **Zeek** for logs and **Suricata** for alerts, then the analysis techniques that sit on top of them.

blocks.code:
# How much disk does a day of monitoring cost? (illustrative model, stated assumptions)
link_bps    = 10e9      # a 10 Gb/s internet link
utilisation = 0.30      # average use over the day, one direction
conns_per_s = 5000      # new connections per second (assumption for a mid-size site)
conn_line   = 400       # bytes per JSON conn.log line (Zeek docs examples: 363 and 370)
day = 86400

pcap_bytes = link_bps * utilisation / 8 * day
conn_bytes = conns_per_s * conn_line * day
print(f"full packets: {pcap_bytes/1e12:6.1f} TB/day")
print(f"conn.log:     {conn_bytes/1e9:6.1f} GB/day")
print(f"ratio:        {pcap_bytes/conn_bytes:6.0f} to 1")
disk = 200e12           # 200 TB of sensor disk for packets
print(f"200 TB holds {disk/pcap_bytes:.1f} days of full packets")

# full packets:   32.4 TB/day
# conn.log:      172.8 GB/day
# ratio:           188 to 1
# 200 TB holds 6.2 days of full packets
blocks.caption: Network speeds are quoted in bits per second, disks in bytes: divide by 8. The numbers are a model with the assumptions in the comments, not a measurement of any real site. It counts one direction: a full-duplex link carries traffic both ways, so a capture of both can double it.

blocks.title: Full packet capture: terabytes per day

scenes.caption: At 10 Gb/s and 30% average use, full capture writes about 32 TB a day (the code above). Drag utilisation and link speed to see how fast it grows.
A 1 Gb/s office link at the same 30% writes about 3.2 TB a day: full capture is affordable at the edge of a small site, painful in a data centre.
A busy 40 Gb/s link at 50% would write over 200 TB a day. This is why big networks keep packets for days, or only for chosen traffic, and keep logs for months.

blocks.md:
So most teams keep **layers with different retention**: packets in a rolling buffer that overwrites the oldest files (days), transaction logs and alerts in a search platform (months), flow records longest of all. An investigation then works backwards: alerts and logs find the moment, and packets, if they still exist, prove the detail.

A note on encryption: most traffic today is TLS (Transport Layer Security). Packets of a TLS session show the handshake and sizes, not the content. That shifts the value towards metadata: names, certificates, timing and fingerprints, which lessons 9 to 13 exploit.

Packets are the most complete evidence and the most expensive to keep. Logs and flows are what you will actually have for anything older than a few days, so design your monitoring around the questions you will need to answer months later.

blocks.prompt: Your sensor keeps 6 days of pcap and a year of Zeek conn.log. Legal asks whether host 10.0.4.17 sent anything to 198.51.100.23 forty days ago, and if so what. What can you answer?
blocks.reveal: You can answer **whether, when and how much**: conn.log has every connection between the two addresses forty days ago, with timestamps, durations, byte counts and the service Zeek recognised. You cannot answer **what** was sent: the packets were overwritten 34 days ago. If the connection was TLS you could not have read the content anyway, but the ssl.log would still give the server name. This is the normal shape of a real investigation.

blocks.question: A team wants to detect a workstation uploading 5 GB to an unknown server at night, across 4,000 hosts, cheaply, and keep a year of history. Which evidence fits best?
options: Flow records or Zeek conn.log, which record bytes per connection
Full packet capture on every link, kept for a year
Suricata alerts only, since a rule will match the upload
Wireshark running on the analyst's laptop
blocks.explain: Volume questions need byte counts per connection, which flows and conn.log record in a few hundred bytes per connection. A year of full packets for 4,000 hosts is enormous. A Suricata rule only fires if someone wrote a rule for this traffic, and a laptop running Wireshark sees only its own traffic.

blocks.question: Why does full packet capture usually lose value against modern HTTPS traffic, even when you can afford to store it?
options: Because pcap files cannot store encrypted packets
Because Wireshark refuses to open TLS traffic
Because TLS hides the content, leaving the handshake, sizes and timing, which logs already summarise
Because HTTPS packets are too large for the snapshot length
blocks.explain: Packets of a TLS session are stored perfectly well, but without the session keys their content is unreadable. What remains (server name, certificate, sizes, timing) is exactly what Zeek and Suricata already record in compact form. Packets still matter for plaintext protocols, for decrypting your own lab traffic, and for proving details.

lessons.title: Capturing at scale: taps, mirror ports, drops and retention

blocks.md:
Before any analysis, a sensor has to receive a faithful copy of the traffic. The prerequisite course introduced the two placements from NIST SP 800-94 (NIST is the US National Institute of Standards and Technology): **inline**, where traffic passes through the sensor so it can block, and **passive**, where the sensor watches a copy. Analysis sensors (Zeek, packet recorders, Suricata in alert-only mode) are almost always passive. The question is where the copy comes from.

Tiny example: a branch office has one 1 Gb/s link to the internet. You want every packet on it. You can ask the switch to copy the traffic to a spare port, or put a small device in the cable itself.

NIST SP 800-94 describes both:

- A **spanning port** (also called a mirror port, or a SPAN port after Cisco's name for the feature, Switched Port Analyzer) is a switch port configured to receive a copy of traffic from other ports. It is "relatively easy and inexpensive", but NIST warns that if the switch is configured wrongly the port "might not be able to see all the traffic", that "when a switch is under heavy loads, its spanning port might not be able to see all traffic, or spanning might be temporarily disabled", and that many switches have only one.
- A **network tap** is "a direct connection between a sensor and the physical network media itself, such as a fiber optic cable", giving the sensor "a copy of all network traffic being carried by the media". Installing one usually needs downtime, and taps have to be bought.
- An **IDS load balancer** (often sold as a packet broker) aggregates copies from several taps or spanning ports and hands each sensor the share or the kind of traffic it should see.

blocks.title: Why a mirror port drops packets when the network is busy

scenes.caption: Simplified model. A full-duplex 1 Gb/s link carries up to 1 Gb/s in each direction at once. Quiet hour: 0.3 Gb/s in plus 0.2 Gb/s out fits easily into a 1 Gb/s mirror port.
Busy hour: 0.8 Gb/s in plus 0.6 Gb/s out. The copy of both directions is 1.4 Gb/s, but the mirror port can only send 1 Gb/s to the sensor.
The switch silently discards the excess, about 0.4 Gb/s here, and the sensor never knows those packets existed. Zeek shows the gaps as missed bytes and capture loss.

blocks.md:
Even with a perfect copy, the sensor itself can lose or distort packets. The FAQ of **Arkime** (an open-source full packet capture and indexing system, formerly called Moloch) lists the usual causes:

- **NIC offloads.** NIC means network interface card. Modern cards "defragment packets or reassemble tcp sessions and pass the results to the host", which is "NOT what we want for packet captures, we want what is actually on the network". Turn those features off on capture interfaces.
- **Ring buffer and MTU.** Raise the card's receive ring to its maximum, and set the capture interface MTU (maximum transmission unit, the largest packet it accepts) to at least 1600, because mirrored traffic often carries extra encapsulation headers.
- **Disk speed.** Network speed is in bits, disk speed in bytes; Arkime advises running at no more than 80% of the disk's measured write speed.

blocks.code:
# Capture interface tuning based on the Arkime FAQ (run on your own sensor)
ethtool -g eth0                               # show the maximum ring buffer size
ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096               # raise the ring buffer
ethtool -K eth0 rx off tx off sg off tso off gso off gro off lro off  # offloads off
ip link set eth0 mtu 1600                     # room for encapsulation headers
blocks.caption: ethtool shows and changes network card settings on Linux. gro and lro (generic and large receive offload) merge incoming packets; with them on, the capture shows giant packets that never existed on the wire. tso and gso do the same for packets the host sends.

blocks.md:
**Measure loss, do not assume it is zero.** Zeek writes a `capture_loss.log` that estimates missing traffic from gaps in TCP sequence numbers; its documentation stresses that a value of 0.41 means 0.41%, not 41%. Per connection, the `missed_bytes` field in conn.log counts bytes Zeek knows it never saw. Suricata writes capture counters (its quickstart shows `stats.capture.kernel_packets`) in periodic EVE stats events. A sensor that silently drops 5% of packets will miss alerts and leave holes in files, and you only find out if you look.

**At scale**, packets go to a recorder that indexes them. Arkime was "created to replace commercial full packet systems at AOL in 2012"; it writes standard pcap files to local disk and sends session metadata to OpenSearch or Elasticsearch (search databases), and it "can scale to handle tens of gigabits/sec". Its pcap retention is simply "based on available sensor disk space". **Security Onion** is a free platform that bundles Suricata, Zeek and the Elastic Stack for a ready-made sensor and analyst console.

blocks.title: A typical monitoring stack at a network edge

scenes.caption: A tap on the internet link copies every packet in both directions, including when the network is busy.
A packet broker (NIST's IDS load balancer) receives the copy and sends it to several sensors, possibly filtered or split by flow.
Zeek, Suricata and a packet recorder such as Arkime each process the same copy. None of them has an IP address on its capture interface (NIST calls this stealth mode).
Logs and alerts flow to a search platform kept for months; packets stay on the recorder's disk for days. Analysts query both.

blocks.md: **Where to put sensors** decides what you can see. A sensor outside the firewall sees attacks that were blocked; one inside sees what got through. A sensor at the internet edge sees internal hosts only after NAT (network address translation) if it sits on the outside of the NAT device, which hides which internal machine made a connection, so place it on the inside or correlate with NAT logs. Traffic between internal hosts (lateral movement) never crosses the edge at all: you need sensors at internal choke points, such as the links into server networks, or host telemetry.

Monitoring captures other people's data. NIST SP 800-86 advises written policies on what may be monitored without approval, a formal request and approval process before recording a particular user's traffic, warning banners on systems, and rules for handling passwords or private messages that analysts see by accident. Capture only networks you own or are authorised to monitor.

blocks.question: Your Zeek sensor on a mirror port shows many conn.log entries with large missed_bytes, but only during the busiest hours. What is the most likely cause?
options: Attackers are deleting packets to hide from the sensor
The switch's mirror port is oversubscribed and drops part of the copy under load
Zeek cannot parse TCP during busy hours
The snapshot length is too small
blocks.explain: NIST SP 800-94 warns that a spanning port may not see all traffic under heavy load. Both directions of a busy link can exceed the mirror port's speed, and the excess is discarded silently. A tap or a faster mirror port fixes it; a snapshot length problem would truncate every packet, not only at busy times.

blocks.question: A capture shows TCP segments of 60,000 bytes on an Ethernet network whose MTU is 1500. What is the best explanation?
options: An attacker is sending oversized packets
Ethernet allows 60,000-byte frames by default
Wireshark joined the packets when it opened the file
The capture was made with large receive or segmentation offload enabled, so the card merged packets before the capture saw them
blocks.explain: Offload features let the card or kernel combine packets into large ones before handing them to the host. The capture then records packets that never existed on the wire. The Arkime FAQ tells you to disable these features on capture interfaces.

lessons.title: Inside a pcap file: headers, snap length, timestamps and integrity

blocks.md:
Every tool in this course reads and writes **pcap** files (packet capture, the "savefile" format of the libpcap library behind tcpdump). Knowing the format byte by byte explains several things analysts trip over: truncated packets, wrong times, and files a tool refuses to open.

Tiny example: a lab file holding two packets, one DNS query and one TCP SYN, is 185 bytes long: a 24-byte file header, then for each packet a 16-byte record header followed by the packet's bytes (75 and 54).

The libpcap `pcap-savefile` manual defines the layout:

- **File header (24 bytes):** a 4-byte **magic number** 0xa1b2c3d4, which also reveals byte order (a reader that sees 0xd4c3b2a1 knows the writer used the opposite byte order, and 0xa1b23c4d means nanosecond timestamps); version 2.4; two unused fields; the **snapshot length**; and the **link-layer type** (1 means Ethernet).
- **Record header (16 bytes per packet):** timestamp seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, then microseconds (or nanoseconds), then the **captured length** and the **original length**.

The snapshot length (snaplen) is the most bytes kept per packet: "packets longer than the snapshot length are truncated". When the two lengths differ, the packet was cut short: you know how big it was, but not what the rest said.

Wireshark and tshark save by default in the newer **pcapng** format (pcap next generation), which can hold several interfaces, per-packet comments and more in one file; its [IETF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng/) notes that libpcap reads only some pcapng files.

scenes.caption: Bytes 0 to 3: the magic number. Written little-endian (least significant byte first), so 0xa1b2c3d4 appears reversed as d4 c3 b2 a1. A reader on a big-endian machine would know to swap every field.
Bytes 4 to 7: version 2.4. Bytes 8 to 15: two fields that writers set to zero and readers must ignore.
Bytes 16 to 19: snaplen 0xffff = 65535, so nothing was cut. Bytes 20 to 23: link type 1, Ethernet: every packet starts with an Ethernet header.
The first record header. 0x6553f100 = 1700000000 seconds (14 November 2023, 22:13:20 UTC), plus 0x0001adb0 = 110000 microseconds.
Captured length 0x4b = 75 and original length 75: the whole DNS packet was kept. The 75 packet bytes follow, then the next record header.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys

with open(sys.argv[1], "rb") as f:
    magic, major, minor, _, _, snaplen, linktype = struct.unpack("<IHHiIII", f.read(24))
    print(f"magic {magic:#x}  version {major}.{minor}  snaplen {snaplen}  linktype {linktype}")
    n = 0
    while hdr := f.read(16):
        sec, usec, caplen, origlen = struct.unpack("<IIII", hdr)
        data = f.read(caplen)
        n += 1
        ethertype = struct.unpack("!H", data[12:14])[0]
        src = ".".join(map(str, data[26:30])); dst = ".".join(map(str, data[30:34]))
        print(f"#{n} t={sec}.{usec:06d} caplen={caplen} origlen={origlen} "
              f"ethertype={ethertype:#06x} {src} -> {dst} proto={data[23]}")

# $ python3 read_pcap.py lab.pcap
# magic 0xa1b2c3d4  version 2.4  snaplen 65535  linktype 1
# #1 t=1700000000.110000 caplen=75 origlen=75 ethertype=0x0800 192.0.2.10 -> 192.0.2.53 proto=17
# #2 t=1700000000.160000 caplen=54 origlen=54 ethertype=0x0800 192.0.2.10 -> 198.51.100.7 proto=6
blocks.caption: A pcap reader in 14 lines, run on a two-packet lab file. It assumes a little-endian file of Ethernet frames carrying IPv4, as lab.pcap is. '<' means little-endian for the pcap headers; '!' means network byte order (big-endian) for the packet's own fields. Protocol 17 is UDP and 6 is TCP.

blocks.code:
$ tcpdump -n -tt -r lab.pcap
reading from file lab.pcap, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet)
1700000000.110000 IP 192.0.2.10.53000 > 192.0.2.53.53: 6699+ A? www.example.com. (33)
1700000000.160000 IP 192.0.2.10.49822 > 198.51.100.7.443: Flags [S], seq 1000, win 64240, length 0

$ shasum -a 256 lab.pcap
57fe571f0fad9de92e6f5a78daed94b064d7629e6691f2ca5e9d1ad955168b32  lab.pcap
blocks.caption: tcpdump decodes the same file: -tt prints the raw epoch timestamps from the record headers, -n skips name lookups. 6699 is the DNS transaction ID 0x1a2b in decimal; + means recursion desired.

blocks.md: **Time is evidence.** A pcap timestamp is the sensor's clock when the packet arrived, recorded as UTC epoch seconds; tools display it in whatever time zone you choose. [NIST SP 800-86](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-86.pdf) (its guide to forensics in incident response) lists a wrong system clock among the common problems with timestamps and recommends NTP (Network Time Protocol) to keep clocks synchronised. If the sensor's clock drifts by five minutes, every timeline you build by merging pcap times with firewall, proxy and host logs is off by five minutes. Check sensor time sync before you need it.

**Integrity is evidence too.** If a capture may end up in a disciplinary case or a court, hash it as soon as you collect it, as above: a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is a fixed-length fingerprint of the file that changes completely if even one byte changes, so it later proves the file is unaltered, record who collected it, when and from where, and work on copies. NIST SP 800-86 also suggests keeping copies of original logs as well as centralised or interpreted copies, in case anyone questions the copying.

blocks.prompt: A capture was made with snaplen 64. A 75-byte DNS packet arrives. What do the two length fields say, and what can an analyst still see?
blocks.reveal: Captured length **64**, original length **75**. The first 64 bytes are kept: the 14-byte Ethernet header, 20-byte IP header, 8-byte UDP header and 22 bytes of the DNS message, which ends partway through the query name. The analyst sees who sent what to whom and how big it was, but not the full name looked up. Small snaplens were common when disks were small; for security work, capture whole packets unless you have a reason not to.

blocks.md: When a tool shows 'packet size limited during capture' or a dissector reports a malformed packet near the end of a frame, compare the captured and original lengths first. Truncation is a property of the capture, not of the traffic.

blocks.question: A colleague's capture tool writes timestamps in nanoseconds. Which field tells a pcap reader to interpret the second time field as nanoseconds rather than microseconds?
options: The link-layer type
The snapshot length
The magic number
The version number
blocks.explain: The pcap-savefile manual says the magic number 0xa1b23c4d (instead of 0xa1b2c3d4) marks a file whose packet timestamps are seconds and nanoseconds. The magic number also reveals the writer's byte order.

blocks.question: Two analysts merge a pcap from a sensor with Windows logs from the victim host. Every network event appears exactly 7 minutes before the matching host event. What should they suspect first?
options: A clock offset between the sensor and the host, so one source must be corrected before building the timeline
The attacker altered the pcap
Packets take 7 minutes to cross a LAN
pcap timestamps are always in local time
blocks.explain: A constant offset across many events is the signature of clocks that disagree. pcap stores UTC epoch time from the sensor's clock, so if either clock is wrong every merged event shifts. Measure the offset from a shared event (such as one known connection), correct it and document the correction.

lessons.title: Wireshark display filters: asking precise questions of packets

blocks.md:
The prerequisite course showed Wireshark's three panes and the difference between a capture filter (decides what is recorded) and a display filter (decides what is shown). This lesson is about writing display filters well, because on a capture of a million packets the filter *is* the investigation.

A display filter is a question about **fields**: named values that Wireshark's dissectors (the decoders for each protocol) extract from every packet. Tiny example: `dns.qry.name.len > 50` shows only DNS packets whose query name is longer than 50 characters, a quick first look for tunnelling. The field names come from Wireshark's [display filter reference](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/); clicking a field in the details pane shows its name in the status bar.

The grammar, from the `wireshark-filter` manual:

- **Existence:** a bare name tests presence. `tls` shows packets with a TLS layer; `http.user_agent` shows HTTP messages that carry a User-Agent header.
- **Comparison:** `==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` (or `eq`, `ne`, `gt` and so on). IP fields accept subnets: `ip.addr == 10.4.19.0/24`.
- **Search:** `contains` looks for a string or bytes; `matches` (or `~`) applies a regular expression (a pattern language for matching text) that is **case-insensitive by default**.
- **Membership:** `tcp.port in {80, 443, 8080}` and ranges such as `{4430..4434}`.
- **Slices:** `eth.src[0:3] == 00:00:83` compares the first three bytes (a vendor prefix).
- **Functions:** `len()`, `count()`, `upper()`, `lower()`, and address tests such as `ip_rfc1918()` for private addresses.
- **Layers:** `ip.src#2` is the source address of the *inner* IP header in tunnelled traffic.
- **Logic:** `not`/`!`, `and`/`&&`, `xor`/`^^`, `or`/`||`, in that order of precedence. Use parentheses rather than relying on it.

**The trap: fields that appear more than once.** In one packet `ip.addr` has two values, the source and the destination. The manual defines `==` as "any field must be equal" but `!=` as "all fields must be not equal". It also adds explicit forms: `===` (all equal) and `!==` (any not equal).

A second trap: every comparison carries a hidden existence test. The manual's example: `ip.dst ne 224.1.2.3` also hides every packet that has no `ip.dst` at all, such as ARP. To hide one address but keep non-IP packets, write `not ip.dst eq 224.1.2.3`.

blocks.title: Evaluating filters against two packets
blocks.code:
ip.addr == 10.0.0.5
ip.addr != 10.0.0.5
ip.addr !== 10.0.0.5
ip.dst ne 224.1.2.3
not ip.dst eq 224.1.2.3
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 && ip.src == 10.4.19.136
tls.handshake.extensions_server_name matches "update"

scenes.caption: Packet A is a DNS query from 10.0.0.5 to 8.8.8.8, so ip.addr holds two values. Line 1: any value equal to 10.0.0.5? Yes, so A is shown.
Line 2: != means all values differ. 10.0.0.5 does not differ, so A is hidden. This is how to remove one host's traffic in both directions.
Line 3: !== means any value differs. 8.8.8.8 differs, so A is shown. Almost every packet passes this filter, which is rarely what anyone wants.
Packet B is an ARP request: it has no IP layer at all. Line 4 needs ip.dst to exist before comparing, so B is hidden even though its destination is not 224.1.2.3.
Line 5 negates the whole test 'ip.dst exists and equals 224.1.2.3'. For B that test is false, so the negation is true and B is shown. The manual recommends this form.
Line 6 combines tests on one packet: a TCP SYN without ACK (a connection attempt) from one host. Line 7 shows TLS ClientHellos whose server name contains 'update', any case.

blocks.code:
tls.handshake.type == 1                          # every TLS ClientHello (type 1)
tls.handshake.extensions_server_name             # ...that carries a server name (SNI)
dns.qry.name.len > 50                            # very long DNS query names
dns.flags.rcode == 3                             # NXDOMAIN answers: the name does not exist
http.request && !http.user_agent                 # HTTP requests with no User-Agent at all
http.request.method in {"POST", "PUT"}           # uploads
http.host matches "^[0-9.]+(:[0-9]+)?$"         # requests addressed to a bare IP
x509sat.UTF8String == "Internet Widgits Pty Ltd" # OpenSSL's default certificate organisation
tcp.port == 443 && tcp.len > 0 && !tls           # payload on 443 that did not parse as TLS
blocks.caption: Hunting filters to try on practice captures. Every field name is from Wireshark's display filter reference. The 'Internet Widgits' filter comes from Unit 42's IcedID walkthrough in lesson 15.

blocks.md:
Two working habits make filters faster:

1. **Build from the packet, not from memory.** Right-click a field in the details pane and choose *Apply as Filter* or *Prepare as Filter*; Wireshark writes the exact field name and value. Then edit.
2. **Add columns for the fields you filter on.** Right-click a field, *Apply as Column*, and the packet list becomes a table of, say, time, source, server name and user agent. Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks' threat research team) recommends customising the columns this way before its Wireshark exercises.

Remember that display filters run after full dissection of the whole file, so on very large captures it is faster to cut the file down first with a capture filter, or with tshark (next lesson).

blocks.prompt: You want packets on TCP port 443 that are not TLS, to find a backdoor that only pretends to be HTTPS. Why does `tcp.port == 443 && !tls` show thousands of innocent packets, and how does the refined filter in the list above help?
blocks.reveal: Most TCP packets carry no TLS at all: handshake SYNs, pure ACKs and FINs have no payload, so they have no TLS layer and match `!tls`. Adding `tcp.len > 0` keeps only packets that carry data. Some innocent ones remain: when one TLS record spans several TCP segments, Wireshark attaches the TLS layer to the last segment and marks the earlier ones as segments of a reassembled PDU (protocol data unit), so they too lack a TLS layer. What is left is a short list to inspect by following the streams.

blocks.md: `ip.addr != X` and `!(ip.addr == X)` both remove every packet to or from X in current Wireshark, but `!==` keeps almost everything. When a filter shows surprisingly many or few packets, check which of the any/all forms you used and whether a hidden existence test removed packets without the field.

blocks.question: You want to hide all traffic to and from your own workstation, 10.0.0.5, to see everything else. Which filter does it according to the wireshark-filter manual?
options: ip.addr contains 10.0.0.5
blocks.explain: != means all values of ip.addr differ from 10.0.0.5, so any packet with 10.0.0.5 as source or destination is hidden. !== means any value differs, which keeps packets with one other address. ip.src != hides only one direction. contains cannot be used on IP addresses, which are atomic fields.

blocks.question: A filter `http.user_agent matches "python"` shows packets whose User-Agent is 'Python-urllib/3.12'. A colleague expected it not to match because of the capital P. Who is right and why?
options: The colleague: matches is case-sensitive like grep
You: matches is case-insensitive by default in Wireshark; add (?-i) to make it case-sensitive
Neither: matches only works on numbers
The colleague: User-Agent values are always lower-cased by the dissector
blocks.explain: The manual says matches applies a PCRE2 (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions) pattern that is case-insensitive by default, and shows (?-i) to force case sensitivity. contains, by contrast, compares exact bytes.

lessons.title: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark

blocks.md:
Opening a large capture and scrolling is the slowest way to find anything. Analysts work from the top down: **overview** (what is in here?), **narrow** (which hosts and conversations matter?), **follow** (what did they say?), **extract** (save the objects and indicators).

Tiny example: a 300 MB practice capture from an infected office. The overview shows 40 hosts; Conversations sorted by bytes shows one workstation pulling 273 KB from a cloud storage site right after a request to a bare IP address; following that stream shows the redirect; exporting the object gives the downloaded archive. Four steps, a few minutes.

blocks.title: The top-down workflow and the Wireshark feature for each step

scenes.caption: Overview: Statistics, Protocol Hierarchy shows the share of packets and bytes per protocol. Odd protocols or a large 'Data' share (payload no dissector recognised) are the first leads.
Narrow: Statistics, Conversations and Endpoints list every pair and every address with packets, bytes, start time, duration and bits per second. Sort by bytes or duration.
Follow: Analyze, Follow, TCP Stream (or TLS, HTTP, HTTP/2, QUIC, the UDP transport under HTTP/3) shows one conversation as the applications saw it, and sets the filter tcp.stream eq N.
Extract: File, Export Objects saves HTTP, SMB (Windows file sharing) and other transferred files; Expert Information lists anomalies such as retransmissions and malformed packets.
Expert Information is, in the user guide's words, 'the starting point for investigation, not the stopping point': its absence does not mean all is well.

blocks.md:
**How Wireshark decides what a packet is.** Each protocol has a dissector, and Wireshark picks the next one using "static routes" (registered port numbers, such as 80 for HTTP) and **heuristic** dissectors that guess from the content, such as a known sequence of bytes at the start of the payload. The user guide warns it "won't know if you use a common protocol on an uncommon TCP port, e.g., using HTTP on TCP port 800". When a stream on an odd port shows as raw `Data`, use **Analyze, Decode As** to tell Wireshark which dissector to apply.

The attacker's view of the same fact: malware often talks on ports chosen for their protocols' reputation (443, 53, 80) and not their content. A dissector that guesses by port will then mislabel traffic, so check what the payload actually is.

**Decrypting TLS in your own lab.** A **key log file** is a text file of per-session secrets that Firefox, Chrome and curl write when the `SSLKEYLOGFILE` environment variable is set (to be precise, their TLS libraries NSS, OpenSSL or BoringSSL do). Wireshark's TLS wiki calls it "a universal mechanism that always enables decryption, even if a Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange is in use". The format is now documented in [RFC 9850](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9850) (July 2026), which is informational and states the format is "intended for use in systems where TLS only protects test data". The older alternative, giving Wireshark the server's RSA private key, works only in limited cases: the wiki lists a session that did not use (EC)DHE key exchange (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman: a fresh key pair for every session), was not resumed, and was not TLS 1.3.

So on a production network you will not decrypt other people's sessions with Wireshark. Where an organisation decrypts at all, it does so at a proxy it controls, under policy.

blocks.title: Decrypting your own browser's TLS with a key log file

scenes.caption: Lab setup: start the browser with SSLKEYLOGFILE pointing to a file, and capture on the same machine.
The TLS handshake crosses the wire as usual. The capture holds ciphertext only.
Meanwhile the browser's TLS library appends the session's secrets to the key log file. Nothing about the network traffic changes.
Encrypted application data flows: HTTP/2 requests and responses inside TLS records.
Wireshark reads the pcap plus the key log file (TLS preference tls.keylog_file) and shows the decrypted HTTP/2 under each TLS record.

blocks.md: A key log file is the key to every session it lists. Treat it like a password file: create it only for test traffic on your own machine, store it with the capture under the same protection, and delete both when done. Never set SSLKEYLOGFILE on a machine others use.

**tshark for scale.** tshark is Wireshark's command-line version: the same dissectors and the same display filter language, without the GUI, so it runs on servers and in scripts. Its native file format is pcapng. The options worth memorising:

- `-r file` read a capture; `-Y 'filter'` apply a display filter; `-q` print only statistics.
- `-T fields -e field ...` print chosen fields as columns, ready for sort, uniq or a spreadsheet.
- `-z io,phs` protocol hierarchy; `-z conv,tcp` TCP conversations; `-z follow,tcp,ascii,N` one stream; `-z expert` expert information.
- `--export-objects http,dir/` save every HTTP object to a directory.
- `-2` two-pass analysis, so fields that need "future knowledge" (like 'response in frame') and reassembly are filled in correctly.

blocks.code:
# Overview: protocol mix and the biggest TCP conversations
tshark -r case.pcapng -q -z io,phs
tshark -r case.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp

# Every TLS ClientHello as a table: time, client, server, name, JA4 fingerprint
tshark -r case.pcapng -Y 'tls.handshake.type == 1' -T fields \
    -e frame.time_epoch -e ip.src -e ip.dst \
    -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name -e tls.handshake.ja4

# Count DNS names per client, most frequent first
tshark -r case.pcapng -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' -T fields -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name \
    | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# Save every object transferred over HTTP (opens nothing, just writes files)
tshark -r case.pcapng --export-objects http,objects/
blocks.caption: Commands to run on your own practice captures. tls.handshake.ja4 exists in Wireshark 4.2 and later (lesson 10 explains JA4). The backslashes continue a shell command on the next line.

blocks.question: A stream to TCP port 8443 shows in Wireshark only as 'Data', but the bytes start with 'GET /update HTTP/1.1'. What is the right next step?
options: Use Decode As to dissect TCP port 8443 as HTTP, then read the requests
Conclude the traffic is encrypted
Delete the packets because Wireshark cannot read them
Re-capture with a larger snapshot length
blocks.explain: Wireshark chose no HTTP dissector because 8443 is not a port it maps to plain HTTP and no heuristic matched. The payload is plainly HTTP, so Decode As fixes the dissection. The user guide gives the same example with HTTP on port 800.

blocks.question: You captured a colleague's HTTPS session to an internal server on the corporate network and want to read it. Which statement is correct?
options: Setting SSLKEYLOGFILE on your own machine lets you decrypt it
Wireshark decrypts TLS 1.3 automatically when Expert Info is enabled
Without that session's secrets, you cannot decrypt it; TLS 1.3 always uses ephemeral key exchange (forward secrecy), so the server's private key does not help
tshark can decrypt it with -2
blocks.explain: Decryption needs the per-session secrets that only the two endpoints know. A key log file from your own machine contains only your own sessions. Wireshark's TLS wiki says RSA private-key decryption does not work with TLS 1.3 or with (EC)DHE key exchange. And beyond the technical answer, reading a colleague's traffic needs authorisation.

lessons.title: Zeek: events, conn.log and protocol detection by content

blocks.md:
**Zeek** is a passive network monitor that turns traffic into structured logs. Its documentation tells the history: Vern Paxson, then a researcher at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), designed the first version in 1995 and called it **Bro**, as an "Orwellian reminder that monitoring comes hand in hand with the potential for privacy violations". In 2018 the project renamed it Zeek, to avoid the connotations of "bro culture"; version 3.0 (2019) was the first release under the new name. You will still meet "Bro" in older papers and scripts.

Tiny example: one HTTP request crosses the wire. Zeek does not raise an alarm. It writes a conn.log line for the TCP connection and an http.log line for the request, linked by the same connection ID, and lets you decide what is interesting.

The [architecture page](https://docs.zeek.org/en/master/about/architecture.html) describes two layers:

1. The **event engine** "reduces the incoming packet stream into a series of higher-level events" that are "policy-neutral": they say what was seen, not whether it matters. Every HTTP request becomes an `http_request` event carrying the addresses, ports, URI and version. Inside, a pipeline does packet analysis (link layer upwards), session analysis (application protocols) and file analysis (files carried inside sessions).
2. The **script interpreter** runs event handlers written in Zeek's own scripting language. "All of Zeek's default output comes from scripts included in the distribution": conn.log, dns.log and the rest are written by scripts, which you can change, extend or add to. Scripts can keep state across connections, raise notices and run external programs.

blocks.title: From packets to logs inside Zeek

scenes.caption: Packets arrive from a capture interface or a pcap file (zeek -r file.pcap).
Packet analysis decodes link, IP and TCP or UDP layers and tracks connections. Session analysis runs the application protocol analyzers chosen for each connection.
The engine emits events such as connection_established, dns_request, http_request and file_new. They describe facts, with no judgement.
Scripts handle the events. The default scripts write the logs; site scripts can add fields, track state and raise notices (notice.log).
Each log line carries the connection's uid, so one connection's records in conn.log, http.log, ssl.log and files.log can be joined later.

blocks.md:
**conn.log in depth.** The prerequisite course used `conn_state` and `history` to spot scans. The other fields matter just as much:

- `uid`: Zeek's unique ID for the connection, used to find related lines in other logs.
- `duration`, `orig_bytes`, `resp_bytes`: how long, and how many **payload** bytes each side sent. `orig_ip_bytes` and `resp_ip_bytes` count whole IP packets, headers included.
- `missed_bytes`: bytes Zeek knows it never saw (gaps in the TCP stream). Non-zero values mean capture loss or asymmetric routing, and any file or content from that connection may be incomplete.
- `service`: the application protocol Zeek **confirmed** by parsing it, which may differ from what the port suggests. Empty means no analyzer recognised the payload.
- `local_orig`, `local_resp`: whether each side is inside the networks you declared as local.

A line is written only when the connection ends or an inactivity timeout expires, so a connection that stays open for hours appears only after it closes. Even after the end, Zeek's docs note the delay "may be up to an hour" when the final FIN or RST was missed, and they point to the zeek-long-connections package, whose conn_long.log first reports a connection after 10 minutes by default.

**Dynamic protocol detection (DPD).** Zeek's documentation: "Rather than selecting which application protocol analyzer to use based on a connection's server port", Zeek uses signatures that "match typical protocol dialogues" to start analyzers, confirms them by parsing, and can "turn off analyzers when it becomes obvious that they are parsing the wrong protocol". Problems are logged in `analyzer.log`.

That gives defenders two strong signals: a known protocol on a port where it does not belong (HTTP on 8080 is normal; HTTP on 53 is not), and a well-known port carrying something no analyzer recognises. The docs' own example is a client that sent a TLS ClientHello to port 443 and got back a plain-text `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request`: the TLS analyzer failed and analyzer.log recorded it.

blocks.code:
$ zeek -r case.pcap LogAscii::use_json=T      # writes conn.log, dns.log ... as JSON lines

# Port 443 connections where no analyzer confirmed a protocol (service is unset)
$ jq -c 'select(."id.resp_p" == 443 and .service == null)
         | {uid, src: ."id.orig_h", dst: ."id.resp_h", duration, orig_bytes, resp_bytes}' conn.log
{"uid":"CbQ2lab0002","src":"10.0.4.33","dst":"198.51.100.23","duration":3605.2,"orig_bytes":48211,"resp_bytes":9204}

# A protocol Zeek recognised on a port other than its usual one
$ jq -c 'select(.service == "http" and ."id.resp_p" != 80)
         | {uid, dst: ."id.resp_h", port: ."id.resp_p", service}' conn.log
{"uid":"CcQ3lab0003","dst":"192.0.2.77","port":8080,"service":"http"}
blocks.caption: jq is a command-line JSON query tool. The jq output is real, run on three lab conn.log lines written for this lesson (Zeek omits unset fields, which jq reads as null). The suspicious line: an hour-long connection to 443 that sent more than it received and never parsed as TLS.

blocks.md: **Case: Operation Aurora (2009 to 2010).** On 12 January 2010 Google [disclosed](https://googleblog.blogspot.com/2010/01/new-approach-to-china.html) that in mid-December it had "detected a highly sophisticated and targeted attack on our corporate infrastructure originating from China", and that "at least twenty other large companies" had been targeted.

[Wired's reporting](https://www.wired.com/2010/01/operation-aurora/) on the analysis by the antivirus company McAfee described the chain: employees visited a malicious website (how they were lured was still unclear at the time) and Internet Explorer was exploited through an unknown flaw (CVE-2010-0249, fixed by Microsoft's out-of-band bulletin MS10-002 on 21 January 2010), malware was downloaded in encrypted stages, and one program opened "an encrypted covert channel that masqueraded as an SSL connection". Data went to command-and-control (C2) servers, which send malware its instructions, in Illinois, Texas and Taiwan; McAfee said the attacks appeared to begin on 15 December and stopped on 4 January, when those servers shut down. McAfee named the operation after a file folder called "Aurora" that the compiler left in the malware.

The network lesson: traffic on port 443 that **is not TLS** stands out to any tool that checks content instead of trusting ports.

blocks.code:
# Suricata: established TCP to port 443 where protocol detection failed
alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 443 (msg:"LOCAL non-TLS traffic on TCP 443"; flow:established,to_server; app-layer-protocol:failed; classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000201; rev:1;)
blocks.caption: app-layer-protocol:failed matches flows where Suricata's protocol detection failed (Suricata rules keyword docs). Zeek's equivalent signal is an empty service field or an analyzer.log entry. Expect some benign hits (custom VPNs, odd appliances): each is worth one look.

blocks.question: conn.log shows a 2-hour connection from a workstation to an internet address on port 443 with service unset, orig_bytes 4.1 MB and resp_bytes 60 KB. Which reading is best?
options: Normal HTTPS browsing: port 443 is always TLS
Worth investigating: no analyzer confirmed TLS, the session is long, and the client sent far more than it received
A capture problem, because unset service always means packet loss
A DNS tunnel, because DNS uses port 443
blocks.explain: Zeek sets service only when an analyzer confirms the protocol by parsing it, so an unset service on 443 means the payload did not look like TLS. A long session that uploads more than it downloads adds to the concern. Unset service does not by itself mean capture loss, but heavy loss can stop an analyzer confirming, so check missed_bytes too.

blocks.question: Why does Zeek write all of its standard logs from scripts instead of hard-coding them in the engine?
options: Because the engine cannot see application protocols
Because scripts run faster than compiled code
Because logs must be written in JSON
So that sites can change, extend or add logs and detection logic without modifying the event engine
blocks.explain: The architecture page says the engine produces policy-neutral events and that 'all of Zeek's default output comes from scripts included in the distribution'. Separating facts (events) from policy (scripts) is what lets each site decide what to log and what to flag.

lessons.title: Zeek's protocol logs and pivoting with uid, fuid and Community ID

blocks.md:
conn.log says that two machines talked. The protocol logs say what they talked about. An investigation moves between them by **pivoting**: taking an identifier from one record and searching for it in other logs.

Tiny example from the Zeek documentation: conn.log shows 192.168.4.37 received 179,604 bytes from 23.195.64.241 on port 80. Its uid, `CzoFRWTQ6YIzfFXHk`, finds the http.log line (the client fetched `wfetch.exe` from `download.microsoft.com`), and the file ID in that line finds the files.log entry (a Windows executable of 179,272 bytes, extracted to disk).
The logs you will use most, with the fields that matter:

- **dns.log**: `query`, `qtype_name` (A, AAAA, TXT, CNAME ...), `rcode_name` (NOERROR, NXDOMAIN ...), `answers` and their `TTLs`, `rtt`. One line per query and response pair.
- **http.log**: `method`, `host`, `uri`, `user_agent`, `status_code`, `request_body_len`, `response_body_len`, and `orig_fuids`/`resp_fuids` and `resp_mime_types` linking to files (MIME types, from Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, are standard format labels such as image/png).
- **ssl.log**: `version`, `cipher`, `curve`, `server_name` (the SNI), `established`, `resumed`, and for TLS 1.2 `cert_chain_fps`, the fingerprints of the certificates the server sent. Zeek's docs show that with TLS 1.3 "there is no mention of certificates in the ssl.log", because TLS 1.3 encrypts them, and that with Encrypted Client Hello even `server_name` disappears.
- **x509.log**: one line per distinct certificate (deduplicated, relogged daily by default), keyed by `fingerprint`, no uid: reach connections via ssl.log. Fields `certificate.subject`, `certificate.issuer`, `certificate.serial`, validity dates, `san.dns` names.

- **files.log**: one line per file seen in any protocol: `fuid`, the carrying connection's `uid`, `source` (HTTP, SMTP, FTP, SMB ...), `mime_type` detected from content, `is_orig` (false means the server sent it), `seen_bytes`, `total_bytes`, `missing_bytes`, and `extracted` if extraction was enabled.

blocks.title: Pivoting through three logs with jq
blocks.code:
jq 'select(.uid=="CzoFRWTQ6YIzfFXHk")' conn.log
# history ShADadtFf, resp_bytes 179604
jq 'select(.uid=="CzoFRWTQ6YIzfFXHk") | {host, uri, user_agent}' http.log
jq '.resp_fuids, .resp_mime_types' http.log
# FBbQxG1GXLXgmWhbk9  application/x-dosexec
jq 'select(.fuid=="FBbQxG1GXLXgmWhbk9")' files.log
# seen 179272, missing 0, extracted HTTP-FBbQxG1GXLXgmWhbk9.exe

scenes.caption: Start from conn.log: one HTTP connection, completed normally (SF), with about 180 KB from the server. Its uid is the key for everything else.
Same uid in http.log: a GET for wfetch.exe from download.microsoft.com, made by Wget on Linux. User agents can be forged, so treat it as a claim.
http.log also names the body's file ID (fuid) and the MIME type Zeek detected from the content: application/x-dosexec, a Windows executable.
The fuid finds files.log: all 179,272 bytes seen, none missing, sent by the server (is_orig false), and extracted to disk under that name.
resp_bytes (179,604) exceeds the file (179,272) by the 332 bytes of HTTP response headers: the numbers agree, so the file is complete.

blocks.md:
**Pivoting between tools.** Zeek's uid exists only in Zeek. Suricata has its own `flow_id`, an endpoint agent has process records, a firewall has its own IDs. Joining them by matching addresses, ports and protocol is tedious and error-prone (which side is the source? what about the reply direction?).

**Community ID**, a specification published on GitHub by the network security company Corelight, standardises a flow hash that every tool can compute the same way: order the two endpoints so the numerically smaller IP:port comes first, concatenate a 2-byte seed, both addresses, the protocol number, a zero byte and both ports in network byte order, hash with SHA-1, base64-encode (write the bytes as text), and prefix the version `1:`. Because of the ordering, both directions of a connection get the same ID. Zeek has supported it natively since version 6.0 (`policy/protocols/conn/community-id-logging.zeek`), and Suricata adds a `community_id` field to EVE records when `community-id: true` is set. The seed must match across all sensors.

blocks.code:
import base64, hashlib, ipaddress, struct

def community_id_v1(saddr, daddr, sport, dport, proto, seed=0):
    s, d = ipaddress.ip_address(saddr).packed, ipaddress.ip_address(daddr).packed
    if (s, sport) > (d, dport):                 # order endpoints: smaller IP:port first
        s, d, sport, dport = d, s, dport, sport
    data = struct.pack("!H", seed) + s + d + struct.pack("!BBHH", proto, 0, sport, dport)
    return "1:" + base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha1(data).digest()).decode()

# Zeek's documentation example: 141.142.228.5:59856 to 192.150.187.43:80 over TCP (6)
print(community_id_v1("141.142.228.5", "192.150.187.43", 59856, 80, 6))
# The reply direction gives the same ID
print(community_id_v1("192.150.187.43", "141.142.228.5", 80, 59856, 6))

# 1:yvyB8h+3dnggTZW0UEITWCst97w=
# 1:yvyB8h+3dnggTZW0UEITWCst97w=
blocks.caption: The output matches the value Zeek's documentation prints for the same flow with its built-in community_id_v1 function. ICMP needs extra mapping of type and code to ports, omitted here.

blocks.prompt: A Suricata alert's EVE record has community_id 1:yvyB8h+3dnggTZW0UEITWCst97w=. What do you search for in Zeek, and what do you expect to find?
blocks.reveal: Search Zeek's conn.log (with community ID logging enabled) for the same string. You expect exactly the connection the alert fired on, in either direction, and from its uid you can pivot to http.log, ssl.log or files.log for the protocol details the alert does not carry. If nothing matches, check that both tools use the same seed, and that the times line up: Community IDs repeat whenever the same 5-tuple is reused, so always match on time as well.

blocks.md: Two IDs carry most investigations: Zeek's uid joins logs about one connection, fuid joins logs about one file. Community ID extends the join to other tools. Learn to move between them quickly; it is most of the job.

blocks.question: An analyst has an ssl.log line for a suspicious TLS 1.3 connection and searches x509.log for its certificate, but finds nothing. Why?
options: Zeek never logs certificates
The certificate is in files.log instead
TLS 1.3 encrypts the server's certificate, so a passive sensor cannot see it unless traffic is decrypted
x509.log only records client certificates
blocks.explain: Zeek's ssl.log documentation shows that with TLS 1.3 there is no certificate information, because the Certificate message is sent after the handshake keys are set. With TLS 1.2 the certificate crosses in clear text and appears in x509.log. The server name (SNI) is still visible unless Encrypted Client Hello is used.

blocks.question: Suricata logs a connection as 10.0.4.17:51000 to 203.0.113.5:443. Your endpoint agent logs the same connection from the server's reply packet, as 203.0.113.5:443 to 10.0.4.17:51000. Will their Community IDs (same seed) match?
options: Yes, because the algorithm orders the endpoints before hashing, so both directions give the same ID
No, because source and destination are swapped
Only if both tools use JSON output
Only for UDP
blocks.explain: The specification removes direction by putting the numerically smaller IP:port first before hashing. That is exactly what makes it useful across tools that disagree on which side started the flow.

lessons.title: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning

blocks.md:
**Suricata** describes itself as "a high performance Network IDS, IPS and Network Security Monitoring engine", open source under the GNU GPL version 2 and developed by the **OISF** (Open Information Security Foundation), a non-profit. The prerequisite course dissected one rule into action, header and options. This lesson covers how those options actually find bytes, what Suricata writes out, and how analysts keep alerts useful.

Tiny example from Suricata's quickstart: with the free **ET Open** ruleset (Emerging Threats Open, a community ruleset) loaded, running `curl http://testmynids.org/uid/index.html` on a monitored host produces the alert `GPL ATTACK_RESPONSE id check returned root`. The test page's body contains the text a Unix `id` command prints for the superuser, and that is what the rule looks for.

blocks.code: alert ip any any -> any any (msg:"GPL ATTACK_RESPONSE id check returned root"; content:"uid=0|28|root|29|"; classtype:bad-unknown; sid:2100498; rev:7; metadata:created_at 2010_09_23, confidence Medium, signature_severity Informational, updated_at 2019_07_26;)
blocks.caption: The real rule from ET Open (emerging-attack_response.rules). |28| and |29| are hex bytes for '(' and ')', so the content is uid=0(root). It watches any IP traffic, so a command's output returning over any protocol can trigger it.

blocks.md:
**How content matching works.** `content` looks for exact bytes, case-sensitive unless followed by `nocase`. Modifiers say where to look:

- `depth:N` checks only the first N bytes; `offset:N` starts looking N bytes in. `startswith` is shorthand for `depth` equal to the pattern's length with `offset:0`.
- `distance:N` (relative) means the next pattern may start anywhere from N bytes after the previous match; `within:N` means it must fall within N bytes after the previous match.
- `bsize` tests a buffer's length, `dsize` a packet payload's size, `pcre` applies a regular expression (slow, so pair it with a content).

**Sticky buffers** point matching at a parsed field instead of raw bytes: after `http.host;`, `tls.sni;` or `dns.query;`, the following `content` applies to that field only. Because Suricata parses the protocol first, `http.host` matches the Host header wherever it appears, and works on any port where HTTP is detected.

blocks.title: Relative content matching on one HTTP request line

scenes.caption: The bytes of a request line, 24 bytes long (sp marks a space). Rule options run left to right, each one searching from where the last match ended.
content:"GET "; depth:4; must lie inside the first 4 bytes. It matches bytes 0 to 3, and the match pointer moves to byte 4.
content:".php"; distance:0; within:10; may start right after byte 3 and must end within 10 bytes of it (byte 13). Found at bytes 6 to 9.
content:"HTTP/1.1"; distance:1; starts searching at least one byte after the .php match. Found at bytes 16 to 23, so all three contents matched.
A variant with content:"id="; offset:20; fails: searching only from byte 20, the bytes are /1.1 and id= appears earlier, at 11 to 13. One failed option means no alert.

blocks.md:
**State across packets.** `flow:established,to_server` restricts a rule to the client-to-server side of a connection that completed its handshake (for UDP, one that has seen traffic both ways). `flowbits` lets one rule set a flag on a flow and another test it later, so a rule can say "this is the second step of something the first rule saw". `threshold` and `detection_filter` count matches before alerting.

**Output: EVE JSON.** EVE (Extensible Event Format) writes one JSON object per line, each with an `event_type`: `alert`, `http`, `dns`, `tls`, `fileinfo`, `flow`, `anomaly`, `stats` and more. Every record for the same flow carries the same `flow_id`, so `jq 'select(.flow_id==...)' eve.json` gathers an alert together with that flow's HTTP request, file information and final flow summary. Enable `community-id` to join with Zeek as well.

blocks.code:
# Local rules: a sticky buffer, a relative match, state, and a threshold

alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"LOCAL HTTP request to a raw IP address"; flow:established,to_server; http.host; pcre:"/^[0-9]{1,3}(\.[0-9]{1,3}){3}(:[0-9]+)?$/"; classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000301; rev:1;)

alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"LOCAL HTTP GET with no User-Agent"; flow:established,to_server; http.method; content:"GET"; http.user_agent; absent; classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000302; rev:1;)

alert tls $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"LOCAL TLS to a server name on the watch list"; tls.sni; dataset:isset,watch-sni, type string, load watch-sni.lst; classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000303; rev:1;)
blocks.caption: Illustrative rules for your own sensor (local sids from 1000000 up). absent checks that a sticky buffer does not exist; dataset matches the buffer against a list loaded from a file (for type string, one base64-encoded value per line). Test every rule against practice pcaps before deploying it.

blocks.md:
**Keeping alerts useful.** A rule is a hypothesis; the first week on real traffic tests it. Analysts deal with noise in three ways:

1. **Tune the rule:** narrow the header (`$HOME_NET` to `$EXTERNAL_NET`), add `flow`, anchor contents with `depth` or sticky buffers.
2. **Threshold or suppress:** `threshold.config` can limit how often a rule alerts, or `suppress` a rule entirely or for specific addresses, for example a vulnerability scanner you run yourself.
3. **Manage rulesets as code:** `suricata-update` is "the official way to update and manage rules"; keep local changes (disabled sids, modified rules) in version control so the next update does not undo them.

Signature detection still has the limit the prerequisite quoted from NIST: excellent on known patterns, weak on new ones. Lessons 9 to 13 cover techniques that do not need a known pattern.

Every Suricata alert should send you to the flow behind it: pull the EVE records with the same flow_id (or the Zeek logs with the same Community ID) and decide from the full conversation, not from the alert message alone.

blocks.question: A rule has content:"admin"; content:".php"; distance:0; within:6;. Which payload makes it match?
options: /admin/login.php
/php/admin
/ADMIN.php
/admin.php
blocks.explain: After matching admin, .php must begin at or after the end of admin (distance:0) and lie entirely within the next 6 bytes (within:6). In /admin.php it follows immediately. In /admin/login.php it starts 6 bytes later and ends 10 bytes after admin, too far. /php/admin has no .php after admin, and /ADMIN.php fails because content is case-sensitive without nocase.

blocks.question: An alert fired on an HTTP response. In eve.json, how do you find that same connection's HTTP request, file information and byte counts?
options: Search for the same signature ID
Select every record with the alert's flow_id
Search for the same timestamp
Read fast.log, which contains the full request
blocks.explain: Suricata gives all records about one flow the same flow_id; its EVE documentation shows jq selecting on flow_id to gather the alert, http, fileinfo, anomaly and flow events together. A signature ID matches every flow that triggered the rule, and timestamps differ between event types.

lessons.title: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3

blocks.md:
Encryption hides content, not behaviour. Before a TLS session has any keys, the client sends a **ClientHello** in clear text: the TLS versions it supports, its list of **cipher suites** (combinations of algorithms) in preference order, and a list of **extensions**, including **SNI** (Server Name Indication, the name of the site it wants), **ALPN** (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation, such as h2 for HTTP/2), the key-exchange groups it supports and the signature algorithms it accepts. The server's **ServerHello** answers with its choices.

Tiny example: two programs connect to the same website. One is a browser, one is a Python script. Both send valid ClientHellos, but the browser sends its own list of ciphers and extensions in its own order, while Python sends whatever its TLS library (usually OpenSSL) offers by default. A sensor that sees only the handshake can already tell the two programs apart.

What a passive sensor can see depends on the TLS version:

- **TLS 1.2:** the ClientHello and ServerHello, and the server's **certificate** in clear text, so Zeek's x509.log and Suricata's `tls.cert_*` keywords work.
- **TLS 1.3** (RFC 9846): the hellos are still visible, but the certificate is encrypted. Zeek's documentation shows the ssl.log keeping only server name, version, cipher and curve.
- **Encrypted Client Hello** (ECH, [RFC 9849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9849), March 2026) encrypts the real ClientHello, including SNI and ALPN, inside an outer one that names only the provider's client-facing server (its `public_name`). The RFC itself notes ECH "is not in itself sufficient to protect the identity of the server": DNS lookups and server IP addresses can still reveal it unless DNS is encrypted too.

The structure of the hello is still visible in every case, which is what fingerprinting uses.

**JA3** turns a ClientHello into a short shareable fingerprint. It was created at Salesforce in 2017 by John Althouse, Jeff Atkinson and Josh Atkins, inspired by the earlier TLS fingerprinting research of Lee Brotherston, author of the FingerprinTLS tool. Its README gives the method: take five fields as decimal numbers, in this order,

`SSLVersion,Cipher,SSLExtension,EllipticCurve,EllipticCurvePointFormat`

joining values inside a field with `-` and fields with `,`, then take the MD5 hash of the string (a 128-bit digest written as 32 hex characters). The README's example `769,47-53-5-10-49161-49162-49171-49172-50-56-19-4,0-10-11,23-24-25,0` hashes to `ada70206e40642a3e4461f35503241d5`. JA3 ignores **GREASE** values (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility, [RFC 8701](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8701)): reserved dummy values such as 0x0a0a and 0x1a1a that browsers insert at random so servers learn to tolerate unknown values. Without that rule, the same browser would produce a new JA3 on every connection.
**JA3S** does the same for the ServerHello (`SSLVersion,Cipher,SSLExtension`). A server answers a given client the same way every time, so the pair JA3 plus JA3S fingerprints the whole negotiation.

blocks.caption: Python's ssl module writes a genuine ClientHello into memory; tls_parse is a 25-line parser (not shown) that walks the record's length-prefixed fields and returns version, ciphers, exts, groups, formats, versions, alpn and sigalgs. Run on your own machine: the result depends on your TLS library.

Same script, same machine, two TLS libraries, two fingerprints. 771 is 0x0303 (TLS 1.2 in the legacy version field; TLS 1.3 support is announced in extension 43). Group 4588 is X25519MLKEM768, the post-quantum hybrid from RFC 10024, which the newer OpenSSL offers first.

blocks.title: From ClientHello fields to a JA3 string (OpenSSL client above)

scenes.caption: Field 1, the legacy version: 771 (0x0303). Every TLS 1.2 and 1.3 client sends this value here, so it rarely distinguishes anything on its own.
Field 2, cipher suites in the client's order: 17 of them, TLS 1.3 suites (4865 to 4867) first. Order and choice are set by the library and the application.
Field 3, extension types in the order sent: 12 extensions, ending with 0 (SNI) and 16 (ALPN). This order is the most distinctive part, and the most fragile (lesson 10).
Fields 4 and 5: supported groups (elliptic curves, now also post-quantum hybrids) and point formats. Joined with commas, the string's MD5 is 72d7d4e38c1ae87df7e249bcfa404051.

blocks.md: **How defenders use it.** The JA3 README lists published examples (with the warning that they are "just examples, not indicative of all versions ever"): the standard client of Tor (the anonymity network) `e7d705a3286e19ea42f587b344ee6865`, Trickbot malware `6734f37431670b3ab4292b8f60f29984`, Emotet `4d7a28d6f2263ed61de88ca66eb011e3`. A rare JA3 seen from one workstation, to a server no one else uses, is a lead.

Althouse's [JA3 and JA3S blog](https://engineering.salesforce.com/tls-fingerprinting-with-ja3-and-ja3s-247362855967/) compares JA3 to the TLS equivalent of a User-Agent string: common software shares fingerprints. Its example: Metasploit's Meterpreter and Cobalt Strike's Beacon (the implants, programs left running on a compromised machine, of two attack frameworks; lesson 11 covers Cobalt Strike) both use the Windows TLS stack, so on Windows 10 they share JA3 values with legitimate programs. What separated them was the **server's** answer: their command-and-control servers, running on Kali Linux (a Linux distribution built for penetration testing) in the blog's tests, replied in a way normal servers did not, so those JA3 values combined with one specific JA3S identified each tool. JA3 is supported by Zeek (as a package), Suricata (`ja3.hash`), Wireshark (`tls.handshake.ja3`), Arkime and many commercial tools.

A fingerprint identifies a TLS library and its configuration, not an intention. Python, Go and Windows programs share fingerprints with malware written in the same language or on the same stack. Use JA3 to cluster and to rank leads, never as a verdict on its own.

blocks.question: Why does JA3 drop GREASE values before hashing?
options: Browsers insert randomly chosen GREASE values, so keeping them would give the same browser a different fingerprint on each connection
They are encrypted and cannot be read
GREASE values only appear in server hellos
RFC 8701 forbids logging them
blocks.explain: GREASE (RFC 8701) reserves values like 0x0a0a that clients add at random to keep servers tolerant of unknown values. They carry no information about the client, and keeping them would make one browser look like many. The JA3 README says it ignores them so programs that use GREASE still produce a single hash.

blocks.question: A TLS 1.3 connection with Encrypted Client Hello crosses your sensor. Which statement is true?
options: You can still read the real server name from the outer ClientHello's SNI
ECH encrypts the IP addresses as well
The real server name and ALPN are encrypted; the outer hello names only the client-facing server, and the server's certificate is encrypted too
ECH only works with TLS 1.2
blocks.explain: RFC 9849 encrypts the inner ClientHello (including SNI and ALPN) and the outer hello carries the public_name of the client-facing server. TLS 1.3 already encrypts certificates. IP addresses are untouched, which is why the RFC says ECH alone does not hide the server's identity.

lessons.title: JA4 and JARM: fingerprints that survive shuffling, and server scans

blocks.md:
JA3 hashes the extensions **in the order sent**. In 2023 that assumption broke. Chromium's feature ["TLS ClientHello extension permutation"](https://chromestatus.com/feature/5124606246518784), enabled by default from Chrome 110, randomises "the order of TLS ClientHello extensions, to reduce potential ecosystem brittleness": Google did not want servers to depend on one fixed order. Every Chrome connection now produces a different JA3. Malware authors had already been doing something similar with ciphers, which the JA4 documentation calls "cipher stunting", randomising cipher order to evade JA3.

Tiny example: take the OpenSSL ClientHello from lesson 9 and shuffle only its extension order, as Chrome does. Same program, same capabilities, new JA3 every time.

blocks.code:
import random
from ja_fingerprints import client_hello_bytes, parse, ja3, ja4

h = parse(client_hello_bytes())
print("original  JA3", ja3(h)[1], " JA4", ja4(h))
random.seed(1)
for i in range(3):                         # extension order randomised, as Chromium now does
    shuffled = dict(h, exts=random.sample(h["exts"], len(h["exts"])))
    print("shuffled  JA3", ja3(shuffled)[1], " JA4", ja4(shuffled))

# original  JA3 72d7d4e38c1ae87df7e249bcfa404051  JA4 t13d1712h2_ab0a1bf427ad_e44827223d20
# shuffled  JA3 0e4b4431432d1637b30f0387faead317  JA4 t13d1712h2_ab0a1bf427ad_e44827223d20
# shuffled  JA3 fa6e906a5b7ab698e9c36bc4bad7382c  JA4 t13d1712h2_ab0a1bf427ad_e44827223d20
# shuffled  JA3 25df8367e657822b0cd19d1e8a214862  JA4 t13d1712h2_ab0a1bf427ad_e44827223d20
blocks.caption: Real output. ja_fingerprints holds the lesson 9 code plus the ja4 function shown below. JA3 changes with every shuffle; JA4 does not, because it sorts the lists before hashing.

blocks.md:
**JA4** (published in September 2023 by FoxIO, the company where JA3's original author John Althouse now maintains his TLS fingerprinting work, and created by Althouse) keeps JA3's idea but fixes its weaknesses. Its format is `a_b_c`:

- **a** is readable: `t` for TLS over TCP (`q` for QUIC, which carries TLS 1.3 over UDP; `d` for DTLS, Datagram TLS); the TLS version, taken from the supported_versions extension when present (`13`); `d` if SNI is present (going to a domain) or `i` if not (going to an IP address); the number of ciphers and of extensions as two digits each, GREASE excluded; the first and last characters of the first ALPN value (`h2`, or `00` for none).
- **b** is the first 12 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the cipher list, written as 4-digit hex and **sorted**.
- **c** is the same for the **sorted** extension list without SNI and ALPN (already in a), followed by `_` and the signature algorithms in their original order.

Sorting removes the randomisation; adding signature algorithms restores uniqueness. And because the parts are separate, you can hunt on part of a fingerprint: the README describes an internet scanner that changed one cipher constantly, producing endless JA3s but a constant JA4 `a` and `c`.

blocks.code:
def ja4(h, proto="t"):
    nog = lambda xs: [x for x in xs if x not in GREASE]
    vers = {0x0304: "13", 0x0303: "12", 0x0302: "11", 0x0301: "10"}
    v = vers.get(max(nog(h["versions"])) if h["versions"] else h["version"], "00")
    sni = "d" if 0 in h["exts"] else "i"
    a1 = h["alpn"][0] if h["alpn"] else ""
    alpn = (a1[0] + a1[-1]) if a1 else "00"
    c, e = nog(h["ciphers"]), nog(h["exts"])
    a = f"{proto}{v}{sni}{min(len(c),99):02d}{min(len(e),99):02d}{alpn}"
    sha12 = lambda s: hashlib.sha256(s.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    b = sha12(",".join(f"{x:04x}" for x in sorted(c)))
    ext_s = ",".join(f"{x:04x}" for x in sorted(x for x in e if x not in (0, 16)))
    sig_s = ",".join(f"{x:04x}" for x in h["sigalgs"])
    return f"{a}_{b}_{sha12(ext_s + ('_' + sig_s if sig_s else ''))}"
blocks.caption: Simplified from FoxIO's JA4 specification: it skips the rules for non-alphanumeric ALPN bytes, DTLS versions and empty lists. Fed the spec's own example lists, the same hashing gives its published parts 8daaf6152771 and e5627efa2ab1.

scenes.caption: t: TLS over TCP. 13: TLS 1.3, read from the supported_versions extension (the legacy version field says 1.2).
d: an SNI extension is present, so the client named a domain. A client connecting straight to an IP address would show i.
17 ciphers and 12 extensions, two digits each, GREASE excluded. These counts alone already separate many applications.
h2: first and last characters of the first ALPN value, h2 (HTTP/2); http/1.1 would give h1. Then come b and c, the sorted-list hashes (first 6 of 12 characters shown).

blocks.md: JA4 itself is open source under the BSD 3-Clause licence, like JA3. The wider **JA4+** family (JA4S for server responses, JA4H for HTTP clients, JA4X for how certificates were generated, JA4SSH, JA4T for TCP and more) is under the FoxIO License, which permits internal use but requires a licence to sell it in a product. Wireshark (4.2 and later) shows `tls.handshake.ja4`; Suricata matches `ja4.hash` and `ja3.hash` as sticky buffers. FoxIO's own warning: fingerprints "will change as application TLS libraries are updated, about once a year", so maintain your lists.

**JARM** (Salesforce, November 2020, also by Althouse with Andrew Smart, RJ Nunnally and Mike Brady) works the other way round: it is an **active** scanner of servers. It sends 10 specially crafted ClientHellos to a server and records which version and cipher the server picks for each, plus its extensions, giving a 62-character fingerprint: 30 characters encoding the 10 choices (`000` for a refusal) and a 32-character truncated SHA-256 of the extensions. Servers built from the same software and configuration give the same JARM.

JARM sends traffic to the server you fingerprint. Scan only servers you own or are authorised to test, or use data from internet scanning services that already publish JARM values. Passive fingerprints (JA3, JA4, JA4S) need nothing but your own sensor.

blocks.question: Since Chrome 110 randomises extension order, which fingerprint of Chrome stays stable from one connection to the next?
options: JA3, because GREASE values are removed
JA4, because it sorts ciphers and extensions before hashing
Neither, all TLS fingerprints are now useless
JA3S, because it covers the client
blocks.explain: JA3 hashes extensions in the order sent, so permutation changes it every time (GREASE removal does not help with ordering). JA4 sorts the cipher and extension lists, so the same set gives the same hash. JA3S fingerprints the server's reply, not the client.

blocks.question: Two clients have JA4 fingerprints t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_e5627efa2ab1 and t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_02713d6af862. What can you conclude?
options: They are the same client
One of them is using QUIC
One connected to an IP address instead of a domain
Same TLS version, SNI use, counts, ALPN and cipher set, but different extensions or signature algorithms: related or similar software, not identical
blocks.explain: Parts a and b match: same protocol, version, SNI presence, counts, first ALPN value and cipher set. Part c differs, so the sorted extensions or the signature algorithms differ. That is the point of JA4's a_b_c design: partial matches carry meaning. QUIC would start with q, and a client going to an IP would show i instead of d.

lessons.title: Case: hunting Cobalt Strike servers by certificate, JARM and quirks

blocks.md:
**Cobalt Strike**, in its own manual's words, "is a platform for adversary simulations and red team operations" (authorised teams who play the attacker). Its documentation is published by Fortra; Recorded Future (a threat intelligence company) described the producer in 2019 as Strategic Cyber LLC and the price as a USD 3,500 licence with annual renewals. An operator runs a **team server**, and compromised machines run its implant, **Beacon**, which checks in over HTTP or HTTPS (the manual describes other channels too). Cracked copies became a staple of criminal intrusions, which is why defenders hunt for its servers.

Tiny example: a workstation makes a small HTTPS connection every minute to an address no one else in the company uses. The certificate that server presents was never changed from the product's default. One field in x509.log is enough to raise the alarm.

[Recorded Future's 2019 research](https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/cobalt-strike-servers) summarised the ways team servers could be found, starting from Strategic Cyber's own "Team Server Population Study" and adding Fox-IT's finding:

- **The default certificate.** Team servers ship with a self-signed certificate (SHA-256 `87f2085c32b6a2cc709b365f55873e207a9caa10bffecf2fd16d3cf9d94d390c`, serial number **146473198**) that identifies them "unless the administrator changes it". Recorded Future judged this "the surest method".
- **Port 50050/TCP**, the default controller port, "a port unlikely to be found open on other servers".
- **The web server's quirks.** The team server's web server was based on NanoHTTPD, an open-source Java web server.
