[Fox-IT](https://blog.fox-it.com/2019/02/26/identifying-cobalt-strike-team-servers-in-the-wild/), a security company, saw an "extraneous space" ending its status line (`200 OK ` before the line break). Using scan data from the security company Rapid7, Fox-IT counted 7,718 hosts with this quirk between January 2015 and February 2019. Cobalt Strike 3.13, released on 2 January 2019, removed the space.

None of these is proof alone: corroboration (default certificate plus open port 50050 plus the NanoHTTPD response) is what Recorded Future used for high-confidence calls.

blocks.title: What a sensor sees when Beacon reaches a default team server

scenes.caption: Beacon opens TLS to the team server. Its ClientHello comes from the Windows TLS stack, so its JA3 matches many legitimate Windows programs.
The server answers. Its ServerHello gives a JA3S; Salesforce's JA3 blog showed that the Windows JA3 values plus one specific JA3S picked out default Cobalt Strike servers.
With TLS 1.2 the certificate crosses in clear text. Zeek's x509.log records serial 08BB00EE (146473198 in hex); Suricata's tls.cert_serial can match it.
Encrypted check-ins follow at the configured interval. Content is hidden, but the rhythm is not (lesson 12).
With TLS 1.3 the certificate is encrypted, so the passive certificate check fails. JA4S, rare-destination analysis, timing, or scan data (JARM, JA4X) take over.

blocks.code:
# Suricata: the default team server certificate (visible with TLS 1.2 and earlier)
alert tls $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"LOCAL Cobalt Strike default certificate serial"; flow:established,to_client; tls.cert_serial; content:"08:BB:00:EE"; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:1000401; rev:1;)

# Zeek: the same serial in x509.log, and certificates with OpenSSL's default organisation
jq -c 'select(."certificate.serial" == "08BB00EE")' x509.log
jq -c 'select(."certificate.subject" | test("Internet Widgits Pty Ltd"))' x509.log

# Python check of the conversion
python3 -c 'print(f"{146473198:08X}")'          # prints 08BB00EE
blocks.caption: Suricata writes serials as colon-separated hex bytes (its docs show 5C:19:B7:...); Zeek writes them as plain hex (find the connections via fingerprint in ssl.log cert_chain_fps). Test both on a practice capture before trusting either: a format mismatch silently matches nothing.

blocks.md:
**JARM at internet scale.** When Salesforce released JARM in November 2020, its README listed Cobalt Strike's default fingerprint, `07d14d16d21d21d07c42d41d00041d24a458a375eef0c576d23a7bab9a9fb1`, with zero overlap with the Alexa top 1 million websites (a popularity ranking) (as of October 2020). An internet-wide scan run with the internet data company SecurityTrails found what the blog believed was "most, if not all" Cobalt Strike servers listening on 443, alongside false positives: Burp Collaborator (another security tool), assorted legitimate servers and a point-of-sale system. JARM fingerprints a server's TLS stack and configuration, so unrelated servers built the same way can share a fingerprint.

The blog's way to separate them is history: "Malicious C2s are generally ephemeral", while legitimate servers keep the same attributes for years. A JARM match on a server that appeared two months ago is far more interesting than one unchanged for over a year.

**Default certificates beyond Cobalt Strike.** Unit 42's IcedID walkthrough (lesson 15) found the malware's command-and-control servers using self-signed certificates with OpenSSL's default values, organisation "Internet Widgits Pty Ltd" and state "Some-State", also seen with other malware such as Bumblebee. Legitimate public sites almost never present such certificates.

**Why these indicators decay.** The **Pyramid of Pain**, from a March 2013 post by David Bianco, a detection specialist, on the blog Enterprise Detection & Response, ranks indicators by how much it hurts an attacker when defenders block them: hash values at the bottom, then IP addresses, domain names, network and host artifacts, tools, and tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) at the top. A default certificate is a network artifact: trivial for a careful operator to replace, but often left alone by careless ones. The JA3 blog makes the same argument for fingerprints: detection "based on the infrastructure and technology, not on destination IPs, domains, or certs" survived the testers moving to new IPs, domains and certificates.

Defenders also act beyond their own networks: in June 2024 the UK's National Crime Agency led an international operation in which 593 of 690 flagged IP addresses running unlicensed Cobalt Strike [were taken down](https://www.nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk/news/national-crime-agency-leads-international-operation-to-degrade-illegal-versions-of-cobalt-strike).

Hunt with layers: a cheap exact indicator (default serial, OpenSSL default subject), a fingerprint of the software (JA3S, JA4S, JARM), and behaviour (timing, rarity, newly seen servers). Each layer catches what the others miss, and corroboration turns leads into findings.

blocks.question: x509.log shows a certificate with serial 08BB00EE on a connection from a finance workstation to an unfamiliar internet address. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore it: certificate serials are random
Block the whole /8 network immediately and close the case
Treat it as a strong lead: list its connections via ssl.log (x509.log has no uid), check other hosts using that address, and seek corroboration such as port 50050 or a recent first-seen date
Re-image every machine in the company
blocks.explain: 0x08BB00EE is 146473198, the default Cobalt Strike certificate serial that Recorded Future called the surest single method. A red-team exercise or a researcher's server could also present it, so you confirm with the connection's behaviour and other hosts' contact with the address before escalating. Blind mass actions without scoping are not a response plan.

blocks.question: Why did Recorded Future and the JARM blog both insist on corroborating indicators rather than acting on a single match?
options: Because each indicator alone has false positives, such as unrelated legitimate servers sharing a JARM or NanoHTTPD servers sharing the extra space
Because indicators are usually wrong
Because the law forbids using one indicator
Because JARM only works on port 50050
blocks.explain: The JARM scan matched Burp Collaborator, a point-of-sale system and other legitimate servers, and Fox-IT's space quirk belonged to NanoHTTPD in general. Combining independent indicators (certificate, port, fingerprint, history) cuts false positives sharply.

lessons.title: Finding beacons with robust statistics: the RITA approach

blocks.md:
Most implants do not hold a connection open. They **beacon**: wake up, ask their command-and-control (C2) server for work, sleep, repeat. Operators add **jitter**, a random variation of each sleep, so the check-ins are not perfectly regular. This lesson builds a regularity score that works on a whole network's logs.

Tiny example: a host contacts one server 60 times in an hour, with gaps between 54 and 60 seconds. Then the laptop's lid closes for an hour, and the next gap is 3,600 seconds. Is it still a beacon? A good score should say yes.

The simple score is the **coefficient of variation** (CV): standard deviation of the gaps divided by their mean. A perfect beacon has CV 0. The weakness is that mean and standard deviation are **not robust**: one extreme value drags both. In the example, the single one-hour gap pushes the CV from 0.03 to 3.92, making a textbook beacon look more irregular than a person browsing.

**RITA** (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics), an open-source tool by Active Countermeasures that "ingests Zeek Logs" and looks for beaconing, long connections and DNS tunnelling, uses statistics built on medians and quartiles instead, which ignore a few outliers:

- **Quartiles** Q1, Q2 (the median) and Q3 split the sorted gaps into four equal groups; the **IQR** (interquartile range) is Q3 minus Q1.
- **Bowley skewness** compares the distances from the median to each quartile: 0 if symmetric, towards +1 or minus 1 if the gaps bunch on one side.
- **MAD** (median absolute deviation) is the median distance of the gaps from their median: a robust measure of spread.

blocks.caption: RITA's timestamp subscore, from its source (analysis/beacons.go). Skewness is taken as 0 when the IQR is under 10 seconds or the median equals a quartile; the MAD term is floored at 0. A score of 1 means perfectly regular.

blocks.code:
import random
from statistics import mean, median, pstdev

def quartiles(xs):
    """Q1, Q2, Q3 as the Go stats library RITA uses computes them (halves exclude the median)."""
    xs = sorted(xs); n = len(xs); h = n // 2
    return median(xs[:h]), median(xs), median(xs[h + n % 2:])

def ts_score(gaps):
    """RITA-style regularity score in [0, 1]: 1 means every gap is identical."""
    q1, q2, q3 = quartiles(gaps)
    skew = (q1 + q3 - 2 * q2) / (q3 - q1) if q3 - q1 >= 10 and q2 not in (q1, q3) else 0.0
    mad = median(abs(x - q2) for x in gaps)          # median absolute deviation
    mad_score = max(0.0, (q2 - mad) / q2) if q2 >= 1 else 1.0
    return round(((1 - abs(skew)) + mad_score) / 2, 3)

random.seed(7)
draw = lambda f, n=59: [f() for _ in range(n)]       # 59 gaps = 60 connections
hosts = {
    "implant, 60 s, 10% jitter": draw(lambda: random.uniform(54, 60)),
    "updater, every 3600 s":     draw(lambda: 3600),
    "random 60 to 180 s":        draw(lambda: random.uniform(60, 180)),
    "person browsing":           draw(lambda: random.expovariate(1 / 120)),
}
hosts["implant + one 1 h sleep"] = hosts["implant, 60 s, 10% jitter"] + [3600]

for name, g in hosts.items():
    q1, q2, q3 = quartiles(g)
    print(f"{name:26s} median {q2:6.1f}s  IQR {q3 - q1:5.1f}  "
          f"CV {pstdev(g) / mean(g):4.2f}  score {ts_score(g):.3f}")
blocks.caption: Synthetic gaps for five host pairs; only the timestamp subscore is shown. RITA computes it per source and destination pair from conn.log.

blocks.code:
implant, 60 s, 10% jitter  median   56.5s  IQR   3.0  CV 0.03  score 0.987
updater, every 3600 s      median 3600.0s  IQR   0.0  CV 0.00  score 1.000
random 60 to 180 s         median  121.9s  IQR  60.7  CV 0.28  score 0.876
person browsing            median   54.3s  IQR 161.5  CV 1.17  score 0.334
implant + one 1 h sleep    median   56.6s  IQR   3.0  CV 3.92  score 0.987
blocks.caption: Real output of the script above. One hour-long gap wrecks the CV (0.03 to 3.92) but leaves the robust score unchanged at 0.987.

blocks.title: Regularity of five host pairs: robust score versus CV

scenes.caption: RITA-style timestamp score (1 = perfectly regular). The implant and the updater top the list; the person browsing scores 0.334.
Coefficient of variation for the same pairs (0 = perfectly regular). One hour of sleep makes the implant look the least regular of all.
Note the updater: perfectly regular and perfectly benign. Regularity ranks candidates; it does not decide what is malicious.

blocks.title: How much does jitter hide a beacon from this score?

scenes.caption: For gaps spread evenly between (1 minus j) times the interval and the interval, the median is I(1 minus j/2), MAD is jI/4 and skew is 0, so the score works out to 1 minus j/(8 minus 4j).
Even at 50% jitter the score is still 0.917, and at 100% (gaps anywhere from 0 to the interval) it is 0.75: uniform jitter is symmetric, so skewness never penalises it.

blocks.md:
Timing is one of four subscores. RITA's default configuration weights each at 0.25: **timestamp** consistency (above), **data size** consistency (the same statistics on bytes per connection: check-ins with nothing to do are all about the same size), **duration** (how much of the dataset's time span the connections cover, and for how many consecutive hours), and a **histogram** subscore (connections spread evenly across the hours of the day, rather than in a burst). A pair needs at least 4 connections before RITA scores it.

**Triage the ranking.** The top of any beacon list is full of benign software: update checkers, antivirus, time sync, monitoring agents, chat clients. Analysts cut it down with:

1. **Prevalence:** how many internal hosts talk to that destination. One host is interesting; 3,000 hosts is an update service.
2. **Age and reputation:** when was the domain first seen in your logs or registered.
3. **Process:** which program made the connections, from endpoint telemetry.
4. **Allowlists:** remove destinations you have already explained, and review the list periodically.

Medians and quartiles let a beacon survive sleeps, reboots and network outages that wreck a mean. Score regularity robustly, then rank by rarity: a regular connection that only one machine in the company makes is the classic lead.

blocks.question: An implant's operator raises jitter from 10% to 50% to avoid detection. Using the formula in this lesson, roughly what happens to its timestamp score?
options: It falls from about 0.99 to about 0.33, the level of a person browsing
It rises to exactly 1.0
It becomes undefined because skewness divides by zero
It falls only slightly, from about 0.987 to about 0.917, so the pair still ranks as very regular
blocks.explain: With 1 minus j/(8 minus 4j): j = 0.1 gives 0.987 and j = 0.5 gives 0.917. Uniform jitter is symmetric, so skewness stays near 0 and only the MAD term drops. Bursty human traffic scores far lower because its gaps are heavily skewed and widely spread.

blocks.question: Your beacon report's top entry: 2,800 internal hosts each contact the same destination every 3,600 seconds exactly, with identical response sizes. What is the best conclusion?
options: A company-wide compromise: isolate all 2,800 hosts
Almost certainly managed software checking for updates or reporting telemetry; verify the destination and owner, then allowlist it so real outliers surface
A DNS tunnel
Capture loss on the sensor
blocks.explain: Very high prevalence plus perfect regularity is the signature of software deployed everywhere, such as an updater. Confirm what it is (destination owner, process on one host) and allowlist it. A real implant usually shows the opposite pattern: regular timing to a destination that only one or a few hosts ever contact.

lessons.title: DNS as a control channel: tunnels, generated names and SUNBURST

blocks.md:
The prerequisite course showed DNS tunnelling query by query: long, random-looking first labels, TXT records, high entropy. At network scale that view drowns in noise: content delivery networks and security products also generate long random-looking names. The more reliable view is **per domain**: how many *different* names under one domain does a client look up, how many clients do it, and is the domain new to you?

Tiny example: in an hour, one workstation looks up `www.example.com` 90 times (one name, many times: normal caching behaviour). Another looks up 120 different names under one domain, each used once. The second pattern is how data moves through DNS, because every new piece of data needs a new name, or the resolver would answer from its cache.

blocks.code:
import random, string
from collections import defaultdict

def base_domain(q):
    return ".".join(q.split(".")[-2:])        # simplified: real tools use the Public Suffix List

random.seed(11)
rand = lambda n: "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase + string.digits, k=n))
log = []                                       # (client, query) pairs, as if read from dns.log
for _ in range(400):
    log.append(("10.0.4.21", random.choice(["www.example.com", "mail.example.com",
                "cdn.example.org", "api.example.org", "login.example.net"])))
for _ in range(120):                            # tunnel: a new long label every query
    log.append(("10.0.4.17", rand(40) + ".t.example.net"))
for _ in range(30):                             # SUNBURST-shaped: short bursts of unique labels
    log.append(("10.0.9.5", rand(random.randint(16, 32)) + ".appsync-api.us-east-1.avsvmcloud.com"))

stats = defaultdict(lambda: {"queries": 0, "names": set(), "clients": set()})
for client, q in log:
    s = stats[base_domain(q)]
    s["queries"] += 1; s["names"].add(q); s["clients"].add(client)

print(f"{'domain':16s} {'queries':>7s} {'unique names':>12s} {'clients':>7s}")
for d, s in sorted(stats.items(), key=lambda kv: -len(kv[1]["names"])):
    print(f"{d:16s} {s['queries']:7d} {len(s['names']):12d} {len(s['clients']):7d}")

# domain           queries unique names clients
# example.net          194          121       2
# avsvmcloud.com        30           30       1
# example.org          154            2       1
# example.com          172            2       1
blocks.caption: Synthetic lab data. Sorting domains by the number of unique names puts the tunnel and the SUNBURST-shaped traffic at the top, even though example.net also carries a normal login name.

blocks.md: **Generated names.** Some malware does not even need a fixed domain. MITRE ATT&CK technique T1568.002 describes **DGAs** (domain generation algorithms) that "dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains", making the channel harder to block or take over. Defenders look for bursts of lookups for never-seen names, many of which fail with NXDOMAIN because the attacker registered only a few of them.

**Case: SUNBURST (2020).** On 13 December 2020 the security company FireEye's Mandiant team [disclosed](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor/) (the analysis now lives on Google Cloud's blog) that SolarWinds' digitally signed Orion IT-management software had shipped a backdoored component, which it named SUNBURST. The same day CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) issued [Emergency Directive 21-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-21-01-mitigate-solarwinds-orion-code-compromise) ordering federal agencies to disconnect affected Orion products, versions 2019.4 through 2020.2.1 HF1. The backdoor's network behaviour is a masterclass in quiet DNS command and control.
What Mandiant's two reports describe:

1. **Patience.** It ran only if its file had been written at least 12 to 14 days earlier ("a dormant period of up to two weeks"), and first checked connectivity by resolving `api.solarwinds.com`, a SolarWinds name that raises no eyebrows on an Orion server.
2. **Generated subdomains.** It resolved DGA-built names under `avsvmcloud[.]com`, ending in one of four suffixes such as `.appsync-api.us-east-1.avsvmcloud[.]com`. The first label joined a victim ID with "a reversible encoding of the victims local machine domain name", so the query itself reported which organisation it was in.
3. **Orders in DNS answers.** The authoritative server for the domain acted as a "C2 coordinator". An A record in certain address ranges meant keep beaconing, others switched the backdoor to active mode, and ranges including 20.140.0.0/15 and the private ranges triggered a permanent **killswitch**. A **CNAME** answer, after an activating A record, named the HTTPS server for real commands.

4. **Irregular timing.** Between generated lookups it waited "any random value from the ranges 1 to 3 minutes, 30 to 120 minutes, or on error conditions up to 420 to 540 minutes". Its HTTP traffic imitated the Orion Improvement Program protocol and waited at least a minute between callouts.

blocks.title: SUNBURST's two-stage control channel (simplified from Mandiant)

scenes.caption: After 12 to 14 dormant days, the backdoor checks connectivity with an ordinary-looking lookup through the company's own DNS resolver.
It resolves a generated name. The resolver forwards it to the attacker's authoritative server: the query itself carries the encoded victim domain.
The answer's IP range is the order. Here: keep beaconing. The backdoor sleeps minutes to hours, then asks again with a new name.
For a chosen victim: an A record in an activating range, then a CNAME naming the HTTPS command server. (These answers also come back through the internal resolver; the arrows skip it.)
Second stage: HTTPS to the CNAME target, disguised as the Orion Improvement Program, at least a minute between callouts.
For uninteresting victims: an A record in a killswitch range (such as 20.140.0.0/15) disables the backdoor for good.

blocks.md:
**What a defender's DNS logs show.** Mandiant recommended "reviewing DNS logs to confirm the presence of a victim's domain in SUNBURST C2 coordinator traffic"; researchers, for example at the security company Kaspersky, [decoded the subdomains](https://securelist.com/sunburst-connecting-the-dots-in-the-dns-requests/99862/) to work out which organisations had been profiled. It also noted that CNAME resolutions for subdomains of avsvmcloud[.]com suggest follow-on activity. In log terms:

- A server that rarely browses (an Orion server) suddenly querying a domain no other host uses, with a **unique name every time**: the per-domain view above flags it, where per-query entropy and timing statistics struggle (minutes-to-hours random waits defeat regularity scores).
- **CNAME answers** for that domain, followed by HTTPS to the named host.

**Where to log DNS matters.** A sensor on the internet link sees the *resolver* making every query. To know which client asked, log at the internal resolver, or put a sensor between clients and resolver. Encrypted DNS to outside resolvers (DoH, DoT) bypasses both, so block or monitor it on managed networks.

Judge DNS by domain, not by query: unique names per domain, clients per domain, first-seen date, and the answer types (TXT, NXDOMAIN, CNAME chains). Tunnels and DGA-driven channels need a new name for every message; normal software keeps asking for the same few names.

blocks.question: Your Zeek sensor sits on the internet link, outside the internal DNS resolver. A DNS tunnel runs from one workstation. What does dns.log show as the client?
options: The internal resolver's IP address, because the resolver makes the outbound query on the client's behalf
The workstation's IP address
The attacker's IP address
Nothing, because Zeek ignores recursive queries
blocks.explain: The workstation asks the internal resolver, which asks the internet. A sensor outside sees only the resolver's queries, so every tunnelled name appears to come from it. Log at the resolver itself or monitor the client side to attribute queries to hosts.

blocks.question: SUNBURST waited a random 1 to 3 minutes, or 30 to 120 minutes, between DNS lookups. Which detection approach suits that best?
options: Timing regularity alone, because the waits are perfectly periodic
Blocking all DNS queries longer than 20 characters
Per-domain analysis: a rare domain receiving a unique subdomain on every query from one server, plus CNAME answers
Looking for port 53 traffic on non-standard ports
blocks.explain: The mixture of random waits from minutes to hours defeats regularity scoring. The DGA, by contrast, must produce a fresh name per query under one parent domain, which per-domain counting exposes. Blocking long names would break many legitimate services, and SUNBURST used normal DNS through the normal resolver.

lessons.title: Extracting files from traffic: reassembly, true types and hashes

blocks.md:
When a file crosses the network in a protocol that is not encrypted (HTTP, SMTP email, FTP, unencrypted SMB file sharing), every byte of it is in the packets. Rebuilding it lets you hash it, check its reputation, and hand it to malware analysts, often before anyone has found the infected host.

Tiny example: the HTTP download from lesson 7. 129 server packets carried 179,604 bytes of TCP payload; strip 332 bytes of HTTP headers and you have the 179,272-byte program, byte for byte. Doing that by hand means reassembling TCP in order, removing headers, undoing chunked transfer encoding and compression. The tools do it for you.

blocks.title: From packets to a file you can hash

scenes.caption: Packets arrive possibly out of order, retransmitted, split at arbitrary points. A file is just bytes spread over many TCP segments.
TCP reassembly puts the stream back in sequence order and removes duplicates. Gaps (lost packets) leave holes that no tool can fill.
The application parser finds where the body starts and ends: HTTP headers removed, chunked encoding joined, gzip undone. Suricata's docs note its HTTP parser does the dechunking and unzipping.
The body is typed from its content (magic bytes), hashed, and optionally written to disk. Each tool logs the metadata even when it does not keep the file.

blocks.md: **Three tools, three styles.**

- **Wireshark, File, Export Objects** lists every object in a chosen protocol (HTTP, SMB, IMF (Internet Message Format) email and others) with the packet number, hostname, content type, size and file name (for HTTP, the last part of the URI), and saves the ones you pick. `tshark --export-objects http,dir/` does the same for all of them at once.
- **Zeek** logs every file it sees in files.log (with `fuid`, `mime_type`, sizes and, if configured, hashes), but its documentation stresses that an entry "does not mean that Zeek necessarily extracted file content": you configure extraction, for example only for MIME type `application/x-dosexec`. Extracted files are named after the source and fuid, such as `HTTP-FBbQxG1GXLXgmWhbk9.exe`.

- **Suricata** extracts files from HTTP, SMTP, FTP, NFS, SMB and HTTP/2 when a rule says `filestore`, logs `fileinfo` records in EVE with hashes, and names stored files by their SHA-256 in directories `00` to `ff`. Its `file-store.stream-depth` setting (1 MB by default, per the documentation) limits how far into a stream it reassembles, so larger files can be truncated unless you raise it.

blocks.code:
import hashlib

# The server's half of one reassembled TCP stream (as Follow TCP Stream would show it)
stream = (b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
          b"Content-Type: image/jpeg\r\n"
          b"Content-Length: 64\r\n\r\n"
          + b"MZ" + b"\x90\x00" + b"\x00" * 60)          # lab stand-in body, not a real program

head, _, body = stream.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")
headers = dict(l.split(b": ", 1) for l in head.split(b"\r\n")[1:])
body = body[:int(headers[b"Content-Length"])]

MAGIC = {b"MZ": "Windows executable (MZ header)", b"%PDF": "PDF document",
         b"PK\x03\x04": "ZIP archive (also docx, xlsx, jar)", b"\xff\xd8\xff": "JPEG image"}
real = next((v for k, v in MAGIC.items() if body.startswith(k)), "unknown")

print("declared type:", headers[b"Content-Type"].decode())
print("magic bytes:  ", body[:4].hex(" "), "=", real)
print("size:         ", len(body), "bytes")
print("sha256:       ", hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest())

# declared type: image/jpeg
# magic bytes:   4d 5a 90 00 = Windows executable (MZ header)
# size:          64 bytes
# sha256:        40517a7274f989a4a9deb13160f0695772bfda13826b4e67a01140ef95432c5a
blocks.caption: Real output. A server can label anything image/jpeg; the first bytes say what the file really is. Zeek's mime_type and Suricata's magic come from the content in the same way, which is why a .jpg that is really a program stands out.

blocks.md:
**Then what?** Hash first, open never. Search the SHA-256 in your threat intelligence, VirusTotal (a service that scans submitted files with many antivirus engines) or MalwareBazaar (a public malware sample database); Zeek's own files.log walkthrough ends by looking a hash up with VirusTotal's command-line tool. Check `missing_bytes` (Zeek) or truncation flags before trusting a hash: a file with a hole hashes differently from the original, so "no results" may only mean "incomplete copy".

**Handle samples safely.** Extracted files may be live malware. Malware-traffic-analysis.net warns there is "a risk of infection if you handle these files on a Windows host" and shares samples only inside password-protected ZIP archives (Unit 42's quiz archive uses the password `infected`), and Unit 42 recommends reviewing malicious Windows traffic from a non-Windows system. Keep samples on an isolated analysis machine and never double-click them.

**Limits.** Nothing can be extracted from HTTPS, encrypted SMB3 or other TLS-protected transfers without the keys. What remains is the size and timing of the transfer, plus the server name, which is why HTTP-only extraction still matters: malware often fetches its next stage over plain HTTP, as the IcedID case in lesson 15 shows.
A hash lookup that returns nothing does not mean a file is safe: new and targeted malware is unknown by definition. Treat unknown executables from unusual sources as suspicious until analysed.

blocks.question: Zeek's files.log shows an HTTP response with mime_type application/x-dosexec, while http.log says the server sent Content-Type image/png. What explains the difference?
options: Zeek misread the file
Zeek types files from their content (magic bytes), while Content-Type is whatever the server chose to claim; an executable disguised as an image is a classic red flag
PNG files always start with MZ
The client changed the type during download
blocks.explain: Content-Type is a header the sender controls. Zeek's file analysis identifies the type from the bytes themselves, so an MZ header marks a Windows executable regardless of the label. The mismatch is worth an alert of its own.

blocks.question: Suricata stored a 4 MB file from a download, but its SHA-256 does not match the vendor's published hash for that file. The sensor shows no packet loss. What should you check first?
options: Whether SHA-256 is broken
Whether the vendor publishes hashes in uppercase
Whether the file was sent over UDP
Whether file-store.stream-depth or the reassembly depth cut the file short
blocks.explain: Suricata's documentation says stored file size depends on file-store.stream-depth and, if that is unset, the stream reassembly depth; beyond it the file can be truncated. A truncated file hashes differently. Compare the stored size with the Content-Length or Zeek's total_bytes.

lessons.title: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation

blocks.md:
In an incident, network evidence answers the questions host evidence cannot answer alone: **which** machine was first, **when** it started, **what** it downloaded, **who else** it talked to, whether it **spread**, and what **left** the network. Hosts can be wiped or lie; a passive sensor that the attacker never touched is an independent witness.

The working method combines everything in this course:

1. **Scope with logs** (months of retention): conn.log, dns.log, ssl.log, alerts. Find every host that touched the indicators.
2. **Confirm with packets** (days of retention): follow streams, export objects, decode what the logs only summarise.
3. **Build one timeline in UTC**, pivoting with uid, fuid and Community ID, and correcting any clock offsets.
4. **Preserve and document**: hash captures and exported files, keep originals, and record every step. NIST SP 800-86 stresses following "consistent processes" and documenting "all actions performed".

**Worked case: Unit 42's IcedID quiz.** Brad Duncan of Unit 42 published a Wireshark quiz in May 2023 built from a real infection in a lab Active Directory (AD, Microsoft's directory service that stores a Windows domain's users and computers) environment, then a full answer walkthrough. **IcedID** (also called BokBot) is Windows malware that, in Unit 42's words, "can lead to ransomware".

The setup given to analysts: LAN segment 10.4.19.0/24, domain `boogienights.live`, a domain controller at 10.4.19.19, three Windows clients, one pcap. The questions: when did the infection start, and what are the infected client's IP address, MAC address, hostname and user account? Is there follow-up activity?

The answers: infection started **19 April 2023 at 15:31 UTC**; client **10.4.19.136**, MAC **14:58:d0:2e:c5:ae**, hostname **DESKTOP-SFF9LJF**, user **csilva**; follow-up: **BackConnect** traffic (a separate channel that, in this pcap, carried the operators' commands).

blocks.title: The IcedID infection chain as the pcap shows it (Unit 42)

scenes.caption: 15:31:08 UTC: the victim's browser sends plain HTTP straight to an IP address, GET /main.php. Requests to a bare IP over port 80 are a classic first lead (filter: http.request plus the client IP).
The response is a 302 redirect to a Firebase Storage URL, a legitimate Google cloud storage service abused to host the payload.

HTTPS to firebasestorage.googleapis.com: about 273 KB flows to the victim. Encrypted, but URLhaus (a public database of malware URLs) had already tagged that URL as IcedID: a password-protected ZIP holding Scan_Inv.exe.
15:35:39 UTC: the installer sends GET / over plain HTTP to skigimeetroc[.]com with no User-Agent and an odd cookie, and receives a gzip binary that becomes the persistent malware.
15:36:41 UTC onwards: HTTPS command and control to two random-looking domains, both with self-signed certificates using OpenSSL defaults (Internet Widgits Pty Ltd).
Later: BackConnect on TCP 443 to 193.149.176[.]100. Following the streams shows encoded data, then a readable command listing the domain's computers, and directory listings of the victim's drives.

blocks.md: **How each answer was found**, using techniques from this course:

- **The start:** filter web traffic for the client and look for HTTP to a bare IP address (lesson 4). Follow the TCP stream to see the redirect (lesson 5).
- **The installer:** the request with no User-Agent stands out (`http.request && !http.user_agent`). Its cookie encodes host details: Unit 42 explains the `_u=` parameter is hex-encoded text.
- **The C2:** the filter `x509sat.UTF8String == "Internet Widgits Pty Ltd"` finds the self-signed certificates (lesson 11), pointing straight at the two C2 IP addresses.
- **BackConnect:** IcedID had moved it from TCP 8080 to 443 that month, "making it harder to find"; following the streams to that IP shows readable commands and output, so it is not an ordinary TLS session (lesson 6: trust content, not ports).
- **Victim identity:** the user from Kerberos (the Windows domain login protocol) with `kerberos.CNameString`, the full name from LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) with `ldap.AttributeDescription == "givenName"`, the hostname from Windows host announcements with `ip contains "DESKTOP-"`, and the MAC from any frame of that IP.

blocks.code:
# IcedID installer cookie from Unit 42's walkthrough: _u=<hex>:<hex>:<hex>
u = "4445534B544F502D534646394C4A46:6373696C7661:46353431423635424230383346354633"
host_hex, user_hex, other_hex = u.split(":")
print("hostname:", bytes.fromhex(host_hex).decode())
print("user:    ", bytes.fromhex(user_hex).decode())
print("third:   ", bytes.fromhex(other_hex).decode(), "(meaning not determined by Unit 42)")

# hostname: DESKTOP-SFF9LJF
# user:     csilva
# third:    F541B65BB083F5F3 (meaning not determined by Unit 42)
blocks.caption: Real output. The malware's own beacon reported the hostname and user the analyst was looking for, in clear text over HTTP. Unit 42 notes the cookie's parameters are unique to IcedID, so they also make a strong network signature.

blocks.md: **From one host to the whole network.** The pcap answered questions about one client. In a real incident you would then take the indicators (the bare IP, the Firebase URL, skigimeetroc[.]com, the two C2 domains and IPs, the BackConnect IP, the OpenSSL-default certificate, the cookie pattern) to months of Zeek and DNS logs: which other hosts contacted any of them, and when? Unit 42's indicator list publishes exactly these values. Indicators near the bottom of the Pyramid of Pain (IPs, domains) change between campaigns, so also hunt for the behaviours: HTTP to bare IPs, requests without a User-Agent, self-signed certificates on new domains, non-TLS traffic on 443.

**Practise legally.** Everything here can be practised without touching anyone else's network:
- Unit 42's [IcedID quiz](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wireshark-quiz-icedid/) and [answers](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wireshark-quiz-icedid-answers/).
- Protocol samples from the [Wireshark sample captures](https://wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures); run Zeek scripts in the browser at [try.zeek.org](https://try.zeek.org/).
- A full sensor and console with [Security Onion](https://securityonion.net/) on your own lab network.
- Network forensics and IDS challenges on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and free rooms on [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/).

Capture and analyse only traffic you own or are authorised to monitor. Practice pcaps of real infections contain working malware and sometimes real personal data from the lab: open them on an isolated, non-Windows machine and never run extracted files.
Network forensics is pivoting with discipline: logs to scope, packets to prove, one UTC timeline, every step recorded. The attacker controls the infected host; they rarely control your sensor.

blocks.question: Which single filter would most quickly show the infected host's first contact with attacker infrastructure in the IcedID pcap?
options: tcp.flags.syn == 1
dns.qry.name contains "microsoft"
http.request with the clients' subnet, looking for requests addressed to a bare IP
tls.handshake.type == 2
blocks.explain: Unit 42 starts with a basic web filter and looks for unencrypted HTTP to an IP address without a domain, which revealed GET /main.php at 15:31:08. SYN packets alone show every connection, ServerHellos (type 2) show every TLS session, and a Microsoft name filter targets nothing in this chain.

blocks.question: After the pcap work, which step turns a one-host answer into an incident scope?
options: Searching months of Zeek, DNS and alert logs for every indicator and behaviour found, to list all hosts that touched them
Re-imaging the infected host immediately
Deleting the pcap to protect privacy
Blocking port 443 at the firewall
blocks.explain: The pcap covers one host for a short window; logs with long retention cover everyone. Searching them for the IPs, domains, certificate pattern and behaviours finds other victims and the first moment of compromise. Containment comes next, informed by that scope; blocking 443 would stop the business, not the attacker.
